notes: PRIVATE — real LSAC questions from disclosure booklets Torren owns. For personal use only. Do not upload to a public repo or share. Explanations, types, difficulty, and trap labels written for this app.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q1
questions.stimulus:
Montoya: Many industrial chemical processes that currently use organic solvents could use ionic liquids instead. Ionic liquids are less hazardous to workers and generate less air pollution. Moreover, some reactions occur at a faster rate or yield smaller quantities of unwanted by-products when ionic liquids are used. So chemical companies should begin using ionic liquids for many reactions that currently use organic solvents.
Peterson: Ionic liquids cost many times as much as organic solvents, so they are currently not practical for the chemical industry.
questions.stem: Of the following, which one, if true, is the strongest counter Montoya could make to Peterson’s argument?

choices.A: The cost of organic solvents is only one of many expenses involved in industrial production of chemicals.
choices.B: New methods for removing by-products of chemical reactions have recently been developed.
choices.C: The chemical industry has historically been quick to adopt new techniques that increase the rate at which reactions occur.
choices.D: Ionic liquids can be reused many times, whereas organic solvents can be used only once.
choices.E: For the sake of public relations, companies will sometimes use a more environmentally friendly process even if it is slightly more expensive.

questions.explanation:
Peterson's argument rests on price per unit: ionic liquids cost many times more. If they can be reused many times while solvents are used once, the effective cost gap shrinks or disappears. That directly counters Peterson.
A — Solvent cost being one of many expenses softens the point a little, but "many times as much" could still be a large added cost. It doesn't touch the per-use comparison the way D does.
B — Better ways to remove by-products help organic solvents, eroding one of Montoya's own advantages.
C — Industry eagerness for faster reactions doesn't answer the cost objection.
E — Companies may pay "slightly" more for PR, but Peterson says ionic liquids cost many times more.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q2
questions.stimulus: The relationship between money and the things it allows one to purchase is like that between a tool and the tasks it enables its user to accomplish. Therefore, since tools are useless if there is no task that needs to be done, _______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?

choices.A: money should be thought of as no more useful than a tool
choices.B: any tool that enables its user to accomplish a task is valuable
choices.C: money is valueless in a world where nothing is for sale
choices.D: money should be regarded as a tool rather than a commodity
choices.E: the value of money derives from the tasks it allows one to accomplish

questions.explanation:
Map the analogy: money : things it purchases :: tool : tasks. Tools are useless with no task to do, so money is useless (valueless) with nothing to purchase.
A — Uses the analogy loosely but draws a ranking ("no more useful") that the parallel doesn't support.
B — About tools, not money. The blank needs the money side of the analogy.
D — Commodity versus tool is a new distinction the argument never sets up.
E — Mixes the two halves of the analogy. Money doesn't "accomplish tasks"; it buys things. And the parallel concerns uselessness without purchases, not where value comes from.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q3
questions.stimulus:
James: The world is increasingly divided between the computer literate and the computer illiterate. The economic gap between rich and poor is partly responsible for causing this division, but the economic gap will widen because of the increasing importance of computer literacy.
Ariel: I disagree. Because of businesses’ increasing need for computer-literate employees, companies will have to train nearly all workers in computer skills. This will lessen the division between the computer literate and the computer illiterate. So whatever might cause the economic gap between rich and poor to widen in the future, it won’t be the importance of computer literacy.
questions.stem: James and Ariel disagree over whether

choices.A: the economic gap between rich and poor will widen
choices.B: the economic gap between rich and poor is now partly responsible for causing the division between the computer literate and the computer illiterate
choices.C: businesses’ need for computer-literate employees will increase
choices.D: the economic gap between rich and poor will widen as a result of the increasing importance of computer literacy
choices.E: companies will have to train their employees in computer skills

questions.explanation:
James says the gap will widen because of computer literacy's growing importance. Ariel: "whatever might cause the gap to widen... it won't be the importance of computer literacy."
A — Ariel allows the gap might widen ("whatever might cause...") and only denies this particular cause.
B — Ariel never addresses what currently causes the division.
C — Ariel asserts it; James never denies it.
E — Only Ariel speaks to training.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q4
questions.stimulus: Overcrowding inclines human beings toward aggressive, competitive behavior. Just consider the behavior of normally considerate people driving in rush-hour traffic or attending crowded sporting events. This shows that, as world population continues to grow, aggressive behavior, including war and crime, will become more frequent and severe.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, strengthens the argument EXCEPT:

choices.A: The frequency and severity of overcrowding in the past have been roughly proportional to the size of world population.
choices.B: The frequency and severity of war and crime have generally increased in the past century, and world population also increased during that period.
choices.C: Some forms of aggressive, competitive behavior, including war, tend to occur even in situations in which human beings are not overcrowded.
choices.D: With respect to its effect on behavior, rush-hour traffic is an example of a situation in which human beings are overcrowded.
choices.E: Most mammals inhabiting a given region exhibit increasingly aggressive, competitive behavior as their population density in that region increases.

questions.explanation:
The argument: overcrowding causes aggression, so more people means more war and crime. Aggression occurring without overcrowding doesn't help that causal story. If anything, it suggests other causes.
A — Ties overcrowding to population size, a link the argument needs. It strengthens.
B — Correlation between population and war/crime over time supports the prediction.
D — Confirms that the rush-hour example really is overcrowding, which supports the evidence.
E — Parallel evidence from other mammals supports density causing aggression.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q5
questions.stimulus: Gahagan’s Greenstore sells a large volume of plants. The vast majority are sold wholesale to commercial buyers, most of them to landscape contractors. Gahagan’s also sells gardening implements, most of which are purchased retail by home gardeners.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: Gahagan’s makes a larger profit from the sale of plants than from the sale of all other products combined.
choices.B: Most of those who make regular wholesale purchases from Gahagan’s have never purchased gardening implements from Gahagan’s.
choices.C: There are more commercial buyers than home gardeners among Gahagan’s regular customers.
choices.D: Gahagan’s sells a few gardening implements wholesale to landscape contractors.
choices.E: A plant purchased from Gahagan’s is more likely to have been purchased by a landscape contractor than by a home gardener.

questions.explanation:
The vast majority of plants go wholesale to commercial buyers, and most of those buyers are landscape contractors. So most plants go to landscape contractors, making any given plant more likely bought by one than by a home gardener.
A — Profits are never discussed.
B — Nothing says whether wholesale buyers also buy implements.
C — Volume of plants isn't the number of customers. A few contractors could buy most plants.
D — Most implements are retail, so some might be wholesale, but nothing says any went to landscape contractors.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q6
questions.stimulus: Anthropologist: During the last ice age, nomadic communities probably needed at least 15 or 20 members to survive, and they were generally not much larger than this. Ice-age nomads are commonly portrayed as primarily big-game hunters, but most of their food must have in fact come from other sources, such as small game and plants. Hunting large animals is a dangerous activity that would have risked the lives of several members of the community.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the argumentation by the statement that ice-age nomads are commonly portrayed as primarily big-game hunters?

choices.A: It is a premise used as support for the overall conclusion of the anthropologist’s argument.
choices.B: It is a clarification of one of the premises of the anthropologist’s argument.
choices.C: It is an objection that the anthropologist raises against an opposing theory.
choices.D: It is the overall conclusion of the anthropologist’s argument.
choices.E: It describes a claim that the anthropologist attempts to refute.

questions.explanation:
"Commonly portrayed as primarily big-game hunters, but most of their food must in fact have come from other sources." The portrayal is what the anthropologist argues against.
A — It isn't support; it's the target.
B — It clarifies nothing.
C — It is the opposing view itself, not an objection the anthropologist raises against one.
D — The conclusion is that most food came from other sources.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q7
questions.stimulus: A truly visual art form—for example, painting—is one in which time plays no essential role. Though it takes time to look at a painting, there is no fixed order in which one must look at its parts, and no fixed amount of time one must spend examining it. In contrast, most art forms, such as poetry and music, are essentially temporal; that is, they require performance, which means they must be experienced in a fixed order and over a roughly fixed amount of time. Poetry, for instance, though often written down and thus seemingly a visual art, actually must be performed, even if the performance is only a silent reading to oneself.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, then on the basis of them which one of the following must be true?

choices.A: Truly visual art forms do not essentially involve performance.
choices.B: Poetry is less like music than it is like painting.
choices.C: Spatiality and temporality are mutually exclusive components of art forms.
choices.D: Art forms that must be examined for an extended period of time in order to be understood are essentially temporal.
choices.E: Anything capable of being performed is either musical or poetic, or both musical and poetic.

questions.explanation:
Performance requires a fixed order and fixed time, so it makes time essential. In a truly visual art, time plays no essential role. So truly visual art can't essentially involve performance.
B — The passage stresses that poetry is temporal like music, the opposite.
C — "Spatiality" is never discussed, and "mutually exclusive" overreaches.
D — Temporal arts require a fixed order and fixed duration. Needing a long time to understand isn't the criterion; painting can take long too.
E — Poetry and music are examples, not an exhaustive list of performable arts.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q8
questions.stimulus: Actors generally learn their lines by focusing on the meanings of the words, the motivations of the characters uttering them, and the physical and emotional dimensions of their own performances. It seems likely that memory can be enhanced by factors such as emotion, action, and context, so this approach is probably more effective than mere rote memorization.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, adds support for the conclusion drawn above EXCEPT:

choices.A: Test subjects are best able to remember items on a shopping list when they are also told how those items will be used.
choices.B: The actors who are able to deliver the greatest amount of dialogue most effortlessly are those who have spent the most time learning their lines.
choices.C: Actors are more readily able to remember lines learned while making an appropriate motion— for example, walking across a stage—than lines learned without an accompanying action.
choices.D: People who try to memorize information by imagining that they are conveying it to somebody else who needs the information show higher retention than those who try to memorize the material by rote.
choices.E: People with no acting experience are able to memorize and deliver lines from a play more accurately after they have read and understood the entire play.

questions.explanation:
The conclusion: meaning-, emotion-, and action-based learning beats rote. That actors who spent the most time learning deliver best says nothing about which method works; it's about time, not approach.
A — Knowing how items will be used is context and meaning. It supports.
C — Action aids memory. It supports.
D — Imagined context beats rote. It supports.
E — Understanding the whole play (meaning) aids memorization. It supports.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q9
questions.stimulus: Journalists often claim that their investigation of the private lives of political leaders is an effort to improve society by forcing the powerful to conform to the same standards of conduct as the less powerful. In reality, however, the tactic is detrimental to society. It makes public figures more concerned with mere appearances, and makes everyone else cynical about the character of their leaders.
questions.stem: The claim that journalistic investigation of the private lives of political leaders is an effort to improve society plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.A: It is a claim that the argument attempts to refute.
choices.B: It mentions a justification that is sometimes offered for a practice that, the argument concludes, has undesirable consequences.
choices.C: It is cited as evidence often given for an assertion that the argument concludes is false.
choices.D: It describes a phenomenon that, according to the argument, is much less damaging to society than journalists often assume.
choices.E: It gives an example of a phenomenon that the argument contends has very different effects from those it is generally assumed by everyone to have.

questions.explanation:
The argument reports journalists' justification for the practice ("an effort to improve society") and concludes the practice is actually detrimental.
A — The argument doesn't deny that journalists intend to improve society. It argues the effects are harmful.
C — It's a justification for a practice, not evidence for an assertion the argument calls false.
D — The argument says the practice is detrimental, not less damaging than assumed.
E — "Assumed by everyone" overstates. It's journalists' claim.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q10
questions.stimulus: While the population of city X is approximately one-half that of city Y, the number of city X residents who are patients in hospitals is only one-fourth that of the number of city Y residents who are patients in hospitals.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, contributes to an explanation of the difference in the number of residents who are patients in hospitals EXCEPT:

choices.A: Preventive health programs are more prevalent in city X than in city Y.
choices.B: The hospitals in city X are noted as leaders in employing outpatient treatment wherever possible.
choices.C: The drinking water of city Y has dangerously high levels of pollutants, whereas this is not the case for city X.
choices.D: The hospitals in city Y are of very high quality, and residents of city X are often sent there for treatment.
choices.E: The lifestyle in city X is significantly less stressful than the lifestyle in city Y.

questions.explanation:
The figure counts city X residents who are hospital patients, wherever the hospital is. X residents sent to Y's hospitals are still X residents in hospitals, so D explains nothing (if anything, it predicts more X patients).
A — Prevention means fewer X residents get sick enough for the hospital. Explains.
B — Outpatient treatment keeps X residents out of hospital beds. Explains.
C — Pollution makes Y residents sicker. Explains.
E — Less stress means healthier X residents. Explains.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q11
questions.stimulus: A law is futile unless most of the parties subject to it abide by it willingly. Thus, there can be no comprehensive international solution to the problem of pollution, since few nations would willingly give up their power over their own industries.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.A: A comprehensive solution to the problems of pollution would require major changes in international law.
choices.B: Some nations would be required to give up some of their power over their own industries as part of any comprehensive solution to the problem of pollution.
choices.C: If most nations were willing to abide by international law, then there could be a comprehensive solution to the problem of pollution.
choices.D: The problems created by pollution affect most of the world’s nations, but the pollution itself is produced by the industries of relatively few nations.
choices.E: Most of the current international laws concerning pollution do not require nations to give up any of their power over their own industries.

questions.explanation:
The argument goes from "few nations would willingly give up power over their industries" to "no comprehensive solution." That works only if a comprehensive solution requires some nations to give up some of that power.
A — "Major changes in international law" isn't what links unwillingness to failure.
C — A sufficient condition for a solution. The argument needs a necessary one.
D — Who produces pollution is irrelevant.
E — Current laws' content doesn't matter.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q12
questions.stimulus: Ecologist: El Niño, a global weather phenomenon that occurs once every several years, is expected to become more frequent in coming decades due to the global warming caused by air pollution. In region T, El Niño causes heavy winter rainfall. Since rodent populations typically increase during long periods of sustained rain, it is likely that average rodent populations in region T will also increase in coming decades.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken the ecologist’s argument?

choices.A: In region T, there is typically much less rainfall in summer than there is in winter.
choices.B: Rodent populations in region T often diminish during long periods in which there are no heavy rains.
choices.C: In many regions that, on average, experience substantially more winter rainfall than region T does, average rodent populations are considerably lower than they are in region T.
choices.D: In region T, winters marked by relatively high rainfall have usually not been marked by long periods of sustained rain.
choices.E: The global warming caused by air pollution produces a number of effects, other than the increase in the frequency of El Niño, that could affect rodent populations.

questions.explanation:
The chain: El Niño → heavy winter rainfall → (assumed) long periods of sustained rain → more rodents. If T's rainy winters usually aren't sustained-rain winters, the last link breaks.
A — Summer rainfall is irrelevant to the winter mechanism.
B — Fewer rodents in dry spells fits the ecologist's model.
C — Other regions' rodent levels involve many other factors.
E — Other effects "could" affect rodents in unknown directions. Too vague to weaken.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q13
questions.stimulus: If the natural history museum stays within this year’s budget, it will be unable to stay within next year’s budget, for renovating next year will make the museum’s expenditures exceed next year’s very tight budget. After all, the museum will have to renovate next year if it does not do so this year, because work from previous renovations is deteriorating rapidly.
questions.stem: The argument’s conclusion can be properly inferred if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: The museum will stay within this year’s budget.
choices.B: This year’s budget is less than next year’s budget.
choices.C: The museum will not renovate next year.
choices.D: The museum will exceed this year’s budget if it renovates this year.
choices.E: The museum will stay within this year’s budget if it does not renovate this year.

questions.explanation:
Conclusion: within budget this year → over budget next year. Premises: no renovation this year → renovation next year → over budget next year. Missing link: within budget this year → no renovation this year, whose contrapositive is renovate this year → exceed this year's budget.
A — Asserting it stays within budget doesn't give the conditional link.
B — Budget sizes don't connect the conditions.
C — Contradicts the chain's assumption that it may need to renovate next year.
E — Gives no renovation → within budget, the reverse of what's needed.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q14
questions.stimulus: Science writer: Scientists often accept a scientific argument largely for social reasons, such as the argument’s acceptance by other scientists or the prestige of the scientist making the argument. But this is not at all to the sciences’ detriment, for similar social factors strongly influence every human endeavor.
questions.stem: The science writer’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: takes for granted that the only legitimate reasons for accepting an argument are social reasons
choices.B: takes for granted that whether a behavior obstructs the achievement of a particular endeavor’s goals depends on the prevalence of comparable behaviors in other endeavors
choices.C: fails to consider the possibility that scientists who accept an argument largely for social reasons also generally consider relevant scientific evidence before accepting the argument
choices.D: fails to consider the possibility that many scientists are unaware that they usually accept scientific arguments largely for social reasons
choices.E: takes for granted that a behavior that is not detrimental to the sciences will not be detrimental to any other human endeavor

questions.explanation:
From "social factors influence every endeavor" the writer concludes they don't harm science. That treats how common a behavior is elsewhere as settling whether it harms this endeavor's goals.
A — The writer says social reasons are common, not that they're the only legitimate ones.
C — That possibility would help the writer, not expose a flaw.
D — Awareness is irrelevant to whether the practice harms science.
E — The writer reasons from other endeavors to science, not the reverse.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q15
questions.stimulus: Historian: Scholars writing histories of an era’s business practices must, of course, analyze the practices and strategies employed by firms of that era. But historians probably study successful firms more frequently than they do unsuccessful firms. Therefore, it is reasonable to think that business histories overestimate the successes of past businesses.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would, if true, most support the historian’s argument?

choices.A: The specific factors that cause businesses to do poorly are often not inferable from historical records of business activity.
choices.B: Those who study past first-person accounts of business strategies inevitably approach them with certain present-day cultural assumptions.
choices.C: The many public legal documents that firms have had to file provide a record that is more objective than that provided by the firms’ own internal documents.
choices.D: The records of businesses that have gone bankrupt are destroyed more frequently than the records of other businesses.
choices.E: Scholars who study businesses of the past are usually trained in the effective techniques of business administration.

questions.explanation:
The argument: oversampling successes leads histories to overstate success. If failed firms' records are destroyed more often, historians are even more likely to study mostly successes. That supports the bias claim.
A — Hard-to-infer failure factors are a different problem from overrepresenting successes.
B — Present-day assumptions aren't about success bias.
C — The objectivity of document types doesn't bear on which firms get studied.
E — Training doesn't affect which firms are studied.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q16
questions.stimulus: Manager: I plan to put together a successful marketing team by choosing highly skilled, independent workers who prefer not to work as part of a tightly knit group. This strategy is bound to succeed because recent research shows that when a common purpose is shared, the flexibility of loosely bound groups enables them to function better than tightly knit ones.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the manager’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.A: presumes that factors that are collectively sufficient for success are also individually necessary for success
choices.B: relies on research that has no apparent relevance to the manager’s proposed plan
choices.C: takes for granted that flexible teams always function significantly better than inflexible teams
choices.D: overlooks the possibility that people who prefer not to work in tightly knit groups may have difficulty committing to a common purpose
choices.E: confuses the goals that the manager is seeking to achieve with the goals that must be held in common by the members of the marketing team

questions.explanation:
The research says loose groups do better when a common purpose is shared. The manager assumes the independent workers will share one. People who dislike tight groups may struggle with exactly that.
A — No sufficient/necessary confusion is involved.
B — The research is relevant; the problem is a missing condition.
C — The manager relies on the research, not on "always significantly better."
E — The manager doesn't conflate personal goals with team goals.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q17
questions.stimulus: Different cultures have independently reached the conclusion that ingesting honey daily promotes vigor and longevity. Thus, unless strong evidence emerges contradicting this conclusion, we should assume that it is true.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.A: Three engineers have inspected the bridge, and each has independently concluded that it is safe. So unless good evidence emerges that the bridge is unsafe, it should be considered safe.
choices.B: Numerous studies have concluded that most people benefit from weight-training exercises. Thus, since no other form of exercise has been shown to be more beneficial, most people should be encouraged to exercise with weights.
choices.C: The members of an independent group of scientists have concluded that human activities over the last century have disrupted global weather patterns. Thus, unless these scientists are working from questionable assumptions, we should conclude that their assessment is correct.
choices.D: Three theater critics, none of whom had any influence on the others, said that Tales in Tokyo was not worth the price of admission. Thus, unless each of these critics happened to attend the play on the same night, it is unlikely that the play will be successful.
choices.E: Several different physicians examined Janet, and none could agree on a diagnosis. Therefore, unless new evidence shows that Janet is unhealthy, she should instead assume that she is healthy.

questions.explanation:
Original: several independent sources agree; so unless strong contrary evidence emerges, accept it. The answer has three engineers concluding independently, then the same "unless" structure.
B — Reasons from no better alternative, not from independent agreement.
C — One group rather than independent sources, and the "unless" clause is about assumptions, not new evidence.
D — Predicts box-office success, a different kind of conclusion, with an odd "unless."
E — Starts from disagreement, not agreement.

traps.B: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure
traps.D: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure
traps.E: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q18
questions.stimulus: Land developer: In a certain nation, stringent regulations prevent private landowners from building on their land if any endangered species is present on it. These regulations make the presence of endangered species a severe financial liability for many landowners and thereby discourage the landowners from protecting the endangered species on their land. Therefore, endangered species would very likely not be harmed by removal of the regulations on land development.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the land developer’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on which one of the following grounds?

choices.A: It confuses a condition whose presence would be required in order for a certain result to be produced with a condition whose presence would be required to prevent that result from occurring.
choices.B: It justifies a claim containing a value judgment solely on the basis of factual claims that do not in themselves entail that value judgment.
choices.C: It unjustifiably overlooks the possibility that even if certain factors tend to produce a given effect, they may be likely to produce stronger countervailing effects as well.
choices.D: It fails to take into account the possibility that policies that are not in the interest of land developers may well be in the interest of landowners.
choices.E: It fails to account for potential reactions from private landowners who do not have any endangered species on their land.

questions.explanation:
The regulations do discourage protection, but they also stop building on habitat. Removing them could cause much greater harm. The developer ignores the countervailing effect.
A — No confusion between conditions that produce and conditions that prevent a result.
B — The conclusion is a factual prediction about harm, not a value judgment.
D — Developers' versus landowners' interests is beside the point.
E — Landowners without endangered species aren't the issue. The problem is what landowners with species could now do.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q19
questions.stimulus: I promised Bernie that I would answer his question. He asked me whether his project had been approved. I misunderstood and thought he had asked whether I had approved it. I said, truthfully, “I would approve it if I could, but I don’t have the authority to do so—that is up to Dorothy, and she hasn’t yet made a decision.” Thus, I fulfilled my promise to Bernie.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.A: All there is to answering a question is giving the questioner the information requested.
choices.B: No person can be held accountable for another person’s decisions.
choices.C: The person responsible for a decision is the one who should explain the decision.
choices.D: One need not fulfill a promise in order to do the best that could be done to fulfill it.
choices.E: Making a promise always obliges a person to keep it.

questions.explanation:
He asked whether his project had been approved. The speaker's reply, that Dorothy hasn't decided, does convey that it isn't approved yet. If answering a question is just giving the requested information, the promise was kept.
B — Accountability for others' decisions isn't the issue.
C — Who should explain the decision doesn't establish the question was answered.
D — Talks about doing one's best instead of fulfilling. The conclusion is that the promise was fulfilled.
E — The obligation to keep promises doesn't show this one was kept.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q20
questions.stimulus: Azalea bushes flourish in acidic soil. Clay soil, while rarely acidic, can be mixed with other types of soil to create a soil that is acidic. Hence, azalea bushes can be made to flourish in clay soil.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?

choices.A: Mixing an acidic soil with another type of soil always results in an acidic soil.
choices.B: Clay soil that is mixed with certain other types of soil is still clay soil.
choices.C: Whenever clay soil is mixed with other types of soil, an acidic soil results.
choices.D: Some plants do not flourish in acidic soil.
choices.E: Azalea bushes do as well in treated clay soils as in naturally acidic soils.

questions.explanation:
The mixture is acidic, but the conclusion says azaleas flourish in clay soil. That holds only if clay soil mixed with other soils still counts as clay soil.
A — "Always" is more than needed. Some mixtures suffice.
C — "Whenever" is more than needed.
D — Other plants are irrelevant.
E — "Do as well" isn't needed; flourishing is enough.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q21
questions.stimulus: Company policy: Eligible employees will be granted up to six weeks of paid parental leave following the birth or adoption of a child. To be eligible, an employee must apply for the benefit at least three months prior to the beginning of the leave period and must have at least one year of full-time employment with the company at the time of application.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the company policy?

choices.A: Mac is a full-time employee who has been with the company for exactly one year. He just adopted a child, and he applied for parental leave three months ago, so Mac should be granted the leave.
choices.B: Sara has worked full-time for the company for three years, and she applied for parental leave four months before the recent birth of her child. However, she should not be granted the leave because she took a leave of absence within the past year.
choices.C: Hal, a second-year, full-time employee, applied for parental leave three months ago. He wishes to stay at home for only two weeks following the impending birth of his child, so the company should not grant him parental leave.
choices.D: Dudley has worked part-time for the company for the past seven years. He applied for parental leave over three months before the birth of his child, so it should be granted to him.
choices.E: Maria has worked full-time for the company for the past two years and applied for parental leave six months prior to her adoption of a child, so she should be granted parental leave.

questions.explanation:
Maria: full-time for two years (at least one year at application), and applied six months ahead (at least three months). Eligible, so the leave should be granted.
A — Mac has been there one year now, so when he applied three months ago he had only nine months. Not eligible.
B — Sara meets both conditions. A past leave of absence isn't a disqualifier in the policy.
C — The policy grants "up to" six weeks, so two weeks is fine. Denial is unwarranted.
D — Part-time employment fails the full-time requirement.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q22
questions.stimulus: An effective acting performance does not call the audience’s attention to the fact that it is a performance. That would make it more difficult for the audience to empathize with the character the actor is playing, and effective dramatic performances do not detract from the audience’s appreciation of a play.
questions.stem: The argument’s conclusion follows logically from the premises if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: An audience will not completely appreciate a play unless all of the acting performances in the play are effective.
choices.B: As long as an acting performance does not call the audience’s attention to the fact that it is a performance, it will not detract from the audience’s appreciation of a play.
choices.C: If a performance by an actor in a play enhances the audience’s appreciation of the play, then the play as a whole is better as a result.
choices.D: An effective dramatic performance in a play will enhance the audience’s appreciation of the play.
choices.E: A dramatic performance that makes it more difficult for the audience to empathize with the actor’s character detracts from the audience’s appreciation of the play.

questions.explanation:
Calling attention to the performance → harder to empathize (premise). Effective performances don't detract from appreciation (premise). Needed: harder empathy → detracts. Then calling attention → detracts → not effective.
A — About full appreciation of the whole play. Doesn't link empathy to detracting.
B — Gives "doesn't call attention → doesn't detract," the wrong direction.
C — Enhancing the play as a whole is a new idea.
D — "Enhance" isn't the same as "not detract," and it doesn't link empathy.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q23
questions.stimulus: The computer software industry is rapidly growing and has been for some time. For a company to grow rapidly, it must be innovative, which means it must have creative employees or a management that is open to new ideas. Logichut is a software company that is said to have no creative employees. If so, its management is evidently open to new ideas.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that it

choices.A: illicitly presumes that because a set of things has a certain property, each member of that set has the property
choices.B: confuses a necessary condition for a company’s being innovative with a sufficient condition for a company’s being innovative
choices.C: illicitly concludes that because many people believe something, it must be true
choices.D: confuses a necessary condition for a company to grow rapidly with a sufficient condition for a company to grow rapidly
choices.E: overlooks the possibility that a software company could have both creative employees and a management that is open to new ideas

questions.explanation:
The industry grows rapidly, and the argument applies the "rapidly growing" requirement to Logichut, assuming a member of the set shares the property of the whole.
B — The conditional about innovation is used correctly (innovative requires creative employees or open management).
C — "Said to have" is reported, but the argument doesn't rely on popular belief.
D — The necessary condition for rapid growth is used correctly. The error is assuming Logichut grows rapidly.
E — Having both wouldn't affect the inference.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q24
questions.stimulus: A movie studio’s script readers discard all proposed scripts that are not submitted by agents, and they discard all scripts that are incorrectly formatted. So a script that is submitted by an agent and formatted correctly will not be discarded by the studio’s script readers.
questions.stem: Which one of the following exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning that most closely parallels that in the argument above?

choices.A: To be accepted, entries in the essay contest must be postmarked by the deadline and accompanied by a completed entry form. March 21 was the deadline. Thus, an entry that is accompanied by a completed entry form but postmarked March 22 will not be accepted.
choices.B: If your kitchen is well organized and you are a good cook, the meals you prepare will be delicious. The dinner Jon prepared last week was not at all tasty, so his kitchen must not be well organized.
choices.C: If Bob starts exercising daily, he will improve his fitness level. His fitness level will also improve if he quits smoking. So if he refuses to exercise and continues to smoke, his fitness level is not going to improve.
choices.D: The police are allowed to ticket any parked car that does not have a parking permit. They are also allowed to ticket any parked car whose parking permit has expired. Thus, the police are going to ticket Ruta’s car, for her parking permit has expired.
choices.E: Most dogs that have attended obedience classes respond correctly to basic commands, but only some are able to perform advanced tricks. Thus, any dog that has attended obedience classes and performs advanced tricks will be able to respond correctly to basic commands.

questions.explanation:
Original: not agent → discard; bad format → discard; so agent and good format → not discarded. That treats two sufficient conditions for discarding as the only ones. Fitness answer: exercise → improve; quit smoking → improve; so neither → no improvement. Same flaw.
A — Both conditions there are necessary for acceptance. The inference is valid.
B — A different error (blaming one of two conditions) with a different structure.
D — Moves from permission ("allowed to ticket") to prediction. A different flaw.
E — Mixes "most" and "some" and builds a different structure.

traps.E: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q25
questions.stimulus: Translator: Dr. Abner, apparently scornful of my translation of an ancient poem on the grounds that it is inaccurate, says that my translation produces in most readers feelings other than those the original text was intended to produce. However, as Dr. Abner should realize, we do not know how people originally responded to the poem or how its author intended them to respond. So Dr. Abner’s criticism is unjustified.
questions.stem: The translator’s argument is flawed in that it

choices.A: fails to adequately address the possibility that the original poem had more than one author
choices.B: draws a conclusion purely on the basis of an appeal to popular opinion
choices.C: fails to adequately address the possibility that the original text was not intended to produce any particular feelings in the reader
choices.D: rejects an argument merely because of the circumstances of the person who offered it
choices.E: concludes that we cannot know that certain effects were not what the author intended merely because we do not know what specific effects the author did intend

questions.explanation:
Abner says readers feel things other than what was intended. The translator says we don't know exactly what was intended or felt. But one can know certain reactions weren't intended without knowing the precise intended ones.
A — Number of authors is irrelevant.
B — No appeal to popular opinion.
C — That possibility would arguably help the translator. Not the flaw.
D — The translator responds to the criticism's substance, not Abner's circumstances.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q26
questions.stimulus: Letter to the editor: In calling on antinuclear activists to “live up to their own ideals” and help find better ways of disposing of nuclear waste, advocates of nuclear power merely prove their own dishonesty. Everyone knows that antinuclear activists want the world rid of nuclear power as soon as possible, and they believe any other option is environmentally irresponsible. But finding better ways of disposing of nuclear waste would probably make nuclear power acceptable to more people and thus likelier to continue.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning in the argument?

choices.A: If other options are available, it is irresponsible to take a possibly beneficial course of action that has the potential of causing harm.
choices.B: It is better to eliminate a potentially harmful practice than to try to improve it, if improving it will not significantly reduce its capacity to cause harm.
choices.C: If one is calling on people to act in a way that will possibly undermine their goals, it is dishonest to ask that they do so for the sake of their ideals.
choices.D: It is irresponsible to try to induce others to find a practice acceptable if it is not one’s own belief that that practice is acceptable.
choices.E: It is dishonest to ask people to live up to their ideals without revealing whether one’s own ideals conflict with theirs.

questions.explanation:
Advocates call on activists to act on their ideals in a way that would likely undercut the activists' goal (ending nuclear power). The principle calls exactly that dishonest.
A — About taking risky actions, not dishonest requests.
B — Compares eliminating with improving. Doesn't speak to dishonesty.
D — About irresponsibility and one's own beliefs, not dishonesty in appealing to others' ideals.
E — About revealing one's own conflicting ideals. The letter's complaint is that the request undermines the activists' goals.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 3 (Reading Comprehension), Q1
questions.stimulus:
Two competing demands we make of the law create a troubling conflict that contributes to the law’s frequent failure to deliver what we imagine it should. On one hand, we want a formalist system of law—one that is rational and rule-based, and that promises to deliver us from arbitrariness, irrationality, and caprice in a coherent, reasoned way. It should be a system that we are capable of understanding and generally able to depend on so that we can order our affairs with the knowledge that none of us will be individually disadvantaged before it. In short, it is imperative that the law provide a universal ordering principle that is rational, consistently applied, and blind to the differing social and economic situations of those who come before it.
On the other hand, however, we want the law to be connected to social reality and sensitive to the particular contexts out of which individual cases arise. After all, a body of law is of little use if it delivers justice that is merely procedural as opposed to substantive—i.e., if it cannot deliver results in individual cases that we can recognize as fair and equitable. It need not, of course, be the outcome that we, as individual parties, would want; someone must, after all, lose in an adversarial system. But it must at least be an outcome that we, as parties and observers, can accept as legitimate and justifiable according to some common understanding of fairness and justice. Cases should not, for example, be decided based strictly on the application of unalterable rules without regard for the equity or reasonableness of the outcome. Such extreme formalism, applied neutrally and without prejudice but also without sensitivity to the social contexts of those involved, speaks little to the substance of justice. And it is imperative that the legal system deliver substantive justice in individual cases— that it derive from and relate to subjective experience as well as objective reason.
It seems, then, that we are left with an irreconcilable tension arising from the competing imperatives of formalism and substantive justice. Any attempt to accommodate both principles within the legal system is bound to fail for systemic reasons: formalism cannot produce substantive justice until there is a reasonable degree of social equality. Without this equality, formalism may very well perpetuate injustice; no universal rules can guarantee otherwise. If we cannot aspire to the significant degree of social and economic equality that is required for formalism to be compatible with the achievement of substantive justice, then formalism should be abandoned so that the law can adapt to social reality. The attempt to reconcile formalism and substantive justice within a legal system situated in conditions of social inequality is a misguided project.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would, if true, most seriously undermine the author’s conclusion about formalism in legal systems?

choices.A: The vast majority of people are quite aware of the imperfections of merely procedural justice but do not see any practical way of remedying these imperfections.
choices.B: Nonformalist legal systems have been found to deliver substantive justice even less frequently than their formalist counterparts.
choices.C: Any type of collective action that is formalized into a set of rules tends to become less effective as those rules become dated and less relevant.
choices.D: Societies in which there is little social inequality tend to use formalism as a basis for their legal systems.
choices.E: A formalist approach to the law is sometimes found to be too broad and abstract to apply to the particulars of individual cases.

questions.explanation:
The author concludes formalism should be abandoned so law can adapt to social reality. If nonformalist systems deliver substantive justice even less often, abandoning formalism would make things worse. That undercuts the conclusion.
A — Public awareness of procedural justice's flaws doesn't bear on whether formalism should be dropped.
C — A general claim about rules becoming dated. Doesn't engage the author's reasoning about inequality.
D — Consistent with the author's view that formalism works only with social equality.
E — Supports the author's criticism of formalism.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the message the author intends to convey in using the phrase “misguided project” in the final sentence of the passage?

choices.A: The project would be much more difficult than the benefits of its success would warrant.
choices.B: Such a project is bound to produce unforeseen negative consequences.
choices.C: The project lacks the expert guidance that would be necessary to make it a success.
choices.D: The steps necessary to make such a project succeed would violate several important principles of justice.
choices.E: Such a project cannot, given the present context, be successful.

questions.explanation:
The author says any attempt to reconcile the two "is bound to fail for systemic reasons" under present inequality. "Misguided" means it can't succeed in this context.
A — Cost versus benefit isn't the author's point. It's impossibility.
B — Unforeseen consequences aren't mentioned.
C — Expert guidance is never discussed.
D — The author doesn't say the steps would violate principles of justice.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following statements about a formalist approach to the law?

choices.A: It tends to be too detailed in its language and is not sufficiently reliant on broad principles.
choices.B: It may satisfy the demands of objective reason and yet fail to connect to social reality.
choices.C: It produces substantive justice in individual cases if it is applied neutrally and without prejudice.
choices.D: Its tension with substantive justice arises from their differing approaches to deductive reasoning.
choices.E: It can be reconciled with substantive justice by formalizing a recognition of social inequalities.

questions.explanation:
Formalism is described as rational and rule-based (objective reason) but, applied without sensitivity to social context, it "speaks little to the substance of justice." It can satisfy reason yet fail to connect to social reality.

C — The passage says neutral, unprejudiced formalism still misses substantive justice.
D — Deductive reasoning isn't discussed.
E — The author says reconciliation is bound to fail under inequality.

questions.stem: The author’s primary purpose in mentioning the fact that someone must lose in an adversarial system of law (third sentence of the second paragraph) is to

choices.A: emphasize the systemic nature of the tension between formalism and substantive justice
choices.B: imply that, invariably, someone will view the outcome of a legal proceeding as unfair
choices.C: suggest that the flaws of formalism may be absent from some systems of law
choices.D: stress that substantive justice cannot be expected to produce outcomes that favor every participant
choices.E: foreshadow the author’s conclusion about the ultimate irreconcilability of formalism and substantive justice

questions.explanation:
In describing substantive justice, the author notes the outcome "need not be the outcome that we... would want; someone must lose." It clarifies that substantive justice isn't about pleasing every party.

B — The author says outcomes should be acceptable as legitimate, not that someone will always see them as unfair.
C — Nothing about some systems lacking formalism's flaws.

choices.A: It cannot be relied upon to deliver results that are recognizably fair and equitable.

choices.C: It adapts too readily to social reality.
choices.D: It takes into account the social and economic circumstances of those who come before the law.
choices.E: It is based on a common understanding of fairness and justice.

questions.explanation:

B — That describes the substantive justice the author wants, not procedural justice.
C — Procedural justice is criticized for being disconnected from social reality.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 3 (Reading Comprehension), Q6
questions.stimulus:
Passage A is adapted from a book review by physicist Freeman Dyson. Passage B is adapted from a response to the review.
Passage A
There are two extreme views concerning the role of science in human understanding. The reductionist view holds that all kinds of knowledge, from physics to ethics, can be reduced to science. The traditional view holds that science is one of many independent sources of knowledge. Most people hold views between these two extremes. Skeptics of paranormal phenomena are generally near the reductionist extreme, while I am near the traditional extreme.
The question of the limits of science is closely connected to the possible existence of paranormal phenomena. Scientific attempts to study extrasensory perception and telepathy have failed. Skeptics conclude from this that paranormal phenomena do not exist. I do not accept this conclusion because I am not a reductionist. Paranormal phenomena may exist but be inaccessible to scientific investigation. This is just a hypothesis, but one that I find tenable and plausible.
This hypothesis is supported by abundant evidence (stories of ordinary people who apparently possess paranormal abilities) collected by the Society for Psychical Research and similar organizations. This evidence is anecdotal rather than scientific, since it cannot be reproduced under controlled conditions. But the organizations have conscientiously interviewed eyewitnesses right after the events and carefully documented the stories. These stories make it clear that if paranormal events occur, they occur only when people are under stress and experiencing strong emotion. This would explain why paranormal phenomena are not observable in well-controlled scientific experiments. Strong emotion and stress are incompatible with scientific procedures.
Paranormal phenomena and the scientific method may be complementary. “Complementary” is a technical term in quantum physics, meaning that two descriptions of nature are both valid but cannot be observed simultaneously. The classic example of complementarity is the dual nature of light. Light behaves as a wave in one experiment and as particles in another, but we cannot see both in the same experiment.
Passage B
Freeman Dyson makes a ridiculous plea for openness to the paranormal because he is not a reductionist and because anecdotal evidence convinces him that under certain conditions (e.g., stress), some people exhibit paranormal powers, unless they are placed in controlled scientific conditions, in which case the powers mysteriously disappear. A scientist of Dyson’s caliber should know that anecdotes do not make a science. The only way to find out if anecdotes represent real phenomena is controlled experimental tests. Paranormal phenomena have repeatedly been subjected to rigorous scientific experiments, and the results are unequivocal: psychic power is a chimera. Dyson recognizes that his belief in the possibility of paranormal phenomena conflicts with his scientific views, but he responds by invoking the principle of complementarity. Sorry, but the principle does not apply to the paranormal. Either people can read other people’s minds or they cannot. Science has demonstrated that they cannot. And being a holist instead of a reductionist or reading about weird things that happen to people does not change this scientific fact.
questions.stem: Both passages are concerned with answering which one of the following questions?

choices.A: Does experiencing apparent paranormal phenomena lead to stress?
choices.B: Is it possible that paranormal phenomena exist?
choices.C: Do anecdotes have any place in scientific inquiry?
choices.D: Is the principle of complementarity valid outside quantum physics?
choices.E: Are there kinds of knowledge that have not been successfully reduced to science?

questions.explanation:
Passage A argues paranormal phenomena may exist despite failed experiments. Passage B argues science has shown they don't. Both address whether they can exist.
A — Neither asks whether paranormal experiences cause stress; A says stress may be a condition for them.
C — Anecdotes come up in both, but as part of the larger question about the paranormal.
D — Only one aspect, and B's dismissal of it is brief.
E — A frames reductionism, but B doesn't address this question directly.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 3 (Reading Comprehension), Q14
questions.stimulus:
In typical accounts of the beginnings of bebop— the first “modern” jazz style, which was originated in the 1940s by Dizzy Gillespie, Charlie Parker, and Thelonious Monk, among others—commercialism plays an important, though indirect, role. By the early 1940s, according to these histories, jazz had reached an impasse. The reigning jazz style, swing, had become “threadbare,” a “harmonic and melodic blind alley,” a formulaic popular music undergoing “death by entropy,” a “billion-dollar rut.”
These metaphors, sampled from various writings on jazz, echo the “crisis theory” of twentieth-century European classical music. Classical music history textbooks commonly impute the eruptions of modernity in the early 1900s to classical music’s stubborn failure to move beyond the language of tonality worn out from overuse in the nineteenth century. Something similar is implied about jazz in the early 1940s. Musicians’ failure to extend jazz’s rhythmic, harmonic, and melodic language in directions plainly indicated by the music itself built up pressure resulting in the eruption of a new musical modernism.
But phrases like “billion-dollar rut” clearly suggest that these writers believe that the real culprit is commercialism—the commingling of art and commerce that had for a time allowed swing to become both an authentic jazz expression and a national fad. Even after swing had run its course, the theory goes, the machinery of the popular music industry continued to prop up the “threadbare” idiom, seducing musicians into going through the motions long after they had any legitimate artistic reason to do so. In other words, mass-market capitalism was a logjam in the path of musical evolution that could be removed only by explosive force. Bebop provided that force. In this version of jazz history there is an implicit teleology to the progression from early jazz through swing to bebop: the gradual shedding of jazz’s associations with dance, popular song, and entertainment. Bebop is the logical culmination of this process—in it jazz became “art,” declaring its autonomy by severing forever its ties to commerce.
This insistence that bebop is anticommercial may suit the needs of contemporary jazz discourse, but it is a poor basis for historical inquiry. It idealizes the circumstances of artistic creation and represses the unpleasant reality that commercial relations permeate all realms of musical entertainment. For the musicians who originated bebop, mass-market capitalism was not a prison from which the true artist was duty-bound to escape, but a system of transactions defining music as a profession, thereby making their achievements possible. By 1945, Parker, Gillespie, and Monk had indeed willed a new musical subculture into being. But they were not trying to disengage from the “commercial” music world so much as to find a new point of engagement with it— one that would grant them a measure of autonomy and recognition.

choices.A: Historical inquiry into the origins of bebop has tended to overemphasize the commercial causes of swing music’s artistic decline.
choices.B: Typical accounts of the origins of bebop misrepresent the relationship of bebop’s originators to mass-market capitalism.
choices.C: Bebop arose as a reaction to the failure of swing musicians to extend jazz’s rhythmic, harmonic, and melodic language in directions plainly indicated by the music itself.
choices.D: Commercial relations permeate all genres of musical entertainment, including bebop.
choices.E: Bebop’s originators did not see bebop as being fundamentally different from swing music.

D — Supports the main point but is narrower.
E — The author never claims this.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 3 (Reading Comprehension), Q16
questions.type: RC: Function / Purpose of a Part
questions.stimulus:
In typical accounts of the beginnings of bebop— the first “modern” jazz style, which was originated in the 1940s by Dizzy Gillespie, Charlie Parker, and Thelonious Monk, among others—commercialism plays an important, though indirect, role. By the early 1940s, according to these histories, jazz had reached an impasse. The reigning jazz style, swing, had become “threadbare,” a “harmonic and melodic blind alley,” a formulaic popular music undergoing “death by entropy,” a “billion-dollar rut.”
These metaphors, sampled from various writings on jazz, echo the “crisis theory” of twentieth-century European classical music. Classical music history textbooks commonly impute the eruptions of modernity in the early 1900s to classical music’s stubborn failure to move beyond the language of tonality worn out from overuse in the nineteenth century. Something similar is implied about jazz in the early 1940s. Musicians’ failure to extend jazz’s rhythmic, harmonic, and melodic language in directions plainly indicated by the music itself built up pressure resulting in the eruption of a new musical modernism.
But phrases like “billion-dollar rut” clearly suggest that these writers believe that the real culprit is commercialism—the commingling of art and commerce that had for a time allowed swing to become both an authentic jazz expression and a national fad. Even after swing had run its course, the theory goes, the machinery of the popular music industry continued to prop up the “threadbare” idiom, seducing musicians into going through the motions long after they had any legitimate artistic reason to do so. Bebop is the logical culmination of this process—in it jazz became “art,” declaring its autonomy by severing forever its ties to commerce.

It idealizes the circumstances of artistic creation and represses the unpleasant reality that commercial relations permeate all realms of musical entertainment. For the musicians who originated bebop, mass-market capitalism was not a prison from which the true artist was duty-bound to escape, but a system of transactions defining music as a profession, thereby making their achievements possible. By 1945, Parker, Gillespie, and Monk had indeed willed a new musical subculture into being. But they were not trying to disengage from the “commercial” music world so much as to find a new point of engagement with it— one that would grant them a measure of autonomy and recognition.
questions.stem: The primary purpose of the reference to eruptions of modernity in classical music in the early 1900s (second sentence of the second paragraph) is to

choices.A: provide evidence that undermines the typical accounts of the origins of bebop by suggesting that factors other than commercialism were at play
choices.B: outline a theory of classical music history that the author claims is parallel to the typical accounts of the origins of bebop
choices.C: suggest that typical accounts of the origins of bebop are based on an inaccurate understanding of the history of twentieth-century music in general
choices.D: describe a movement in classical music that was part of the impetus behind the transition from swing to bebop in jazz

questions.stem: Which one of the following principles does the author use in analyzing typical accounts of the origins of bebop?

choices.A: Artistic progress in music is generally the result of commercial pressures.
choices.B: New movements in music typically begin with the rejection of the fundamental principles of the reigning musical style.
choices.C: Music historians should rely primarily on musicians’ first-hand accounts in analyzing significant developments in music.
choices.D: The turns of phrase employed by historians can legitimately be analyzed to uncover the historians’ assumptions.

questions.location: January 2023 LSAT Disclosure, Section 3 (Reading Comprehension), Q22
questions.stimulus:
Organic chemist Larry Koskan’s inspiration arrived in the mid-1980s, when he read a report by marine biologists describing how oyster shells grow. It was known that oysters secrete calcium carbonate as an essential constituent of their hardened exteriors, but the biologists discovered that they also produce a special protein-based agent that molds the mineral into their shells’ characteristic shape.
At the time, Koskan was studying the properties of water-soluble polyacrylates. Among other things, these widely used additives help to stem the buildup of damaging mineral-scale deposits (carbonate and sulphate compounds) on the surfaces of industrial water-treatment equipment. What Koskan realized was that the agent produced by the oysters—polyaspartate— inhibits the formation of calcium carbonate and could also therefore control scale. Polyaspartate mimics the scale-inhibiting activity of polyacrylates because it has a similar chemical structure. But because the backbone of polyaspartate is made of peptides (chains of amino acids) rather than the hydrocarbon compounds that constitute polyacrylates’ backbone, it is subject to bacterial action (i.e., it is biodegradable).
Polyacrylates, inexpensive and versatile chemicals, are easy to manufacture and process. In laundry detergents, they act as dispersants that keep dirt suspended in the wash water. As a recent alternative to phosphates, which, via wastewater, pollute surface waters, some half a billion pounds of polyacrylates are used in detergents worldwide every year. Additionally, some polyacrylates have chemical configurations with a tremendous affinity for water, making them ideal in superabsorbent materials for disposable products like baby diapers, which currently account for around 2 billion pounds in annual production of polyacrylates. The trouble is, polyacrylates last virtually forever, and these vast quantities of the highly stable substance are being discarded in landfills.
With requests by consumer products companies for environmentally friendly products growing rapidly, Koskan started his own small company and began researching cost-effective ways of producing polyaspartate for industrial use. Soon, leading chemical companies also began researching the issue, with the consensus being that polyaspartate was the most suitable replacement for polyacrylates. Unfortunately, as with many emerging technologies that lack a supporting infrastructure, polyaspartate’s price was estimated to be four to five times that of the high-volume-production alternative. Given this, the consumer products industry lost interest in the technology, and the chemical industry shelved it. Koskan’s company, however, believing that polyaspartate could nonetheless be market-competitive on its own merits, decided to persevere and focus on specialty application niches. Polyaspartate has since shown unparalleled success at eliminating scale in offshore oil production equipment and is being used by the farming industry to keep chemical fertilizers in the soil longer, reducing pollution of groundwater by the fertilizers. If Koskan’s company can show continued success, it may yet help enliven an environmental chemistry sector saddled with a reputation for ineffectiveness and high cost.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.A: Polyaspartate was once thought to be the inevitable successor to polyacrylates, but technical shortcomings restrict its usefulness to applications in specialized niche markets.
choices.B: The success of Koskan’s company in the development of polyaspartate for industrial uses may improve the reputation of the environmental chemical industry.
choices.C: Polyaspartate, which Koskan researched and developed as an environmentally friendly alternative to polyacrylates, shows promise for commercial applications but also faces barriers.
choices.D: Koskan’s work with polyaspartate has shown that environmentally friendly alternatives to many industrial chemicals can be found by studying plants and animals.
choices.E: Although polyaspartate is superior to existing products, it will probably fail in the marketplace because of hurdles that stand in the way of its being economically competitive.

questions.explanation:
The passage traces polyaspartate's development, its environmental promise, its cost barriers, and its niche successes. Promise and barriers.
A — The barrier was cost, not technical shortcomings, and niche success isn't framed as a restriction.
B — The final sentence's speculation, not the main point.
D — One example doesn't show alternatives to "many" chemicals can be found this way.
E — The passage ends on success in niches and possible broader impact.

But because the backbone of polyaspartate is made of peptides (chains of amino acids) rather than the hydrocarbon compounds that constitute polyacrylates’ backbone, it is subject to bacterial action (i.e., it is biodegradable).
Polyacrylates, inexpensive and versatile chemicals, are easy to manufacture and process. In laundry detergents, they act as dispersants that keep dirt suspended in the wash water. As a recent alternative to phosphates, which, via wastewater, pollute surface waters, some half a billion pounds of polyacrylates are used in detergents worldwide every year. Additionally, some polyacrylates have chemical configurations with a tremendous affinity for water, making them ideal in superabsorbent materials for disposable products like baby diapers, which currently account for around 2 billion pounds in annual production of polyacrylates. The trouble is, polyacrylates last virtually forever, and these vast quantities of the highly stable substance are being discarded in landfills.
With requests by consumer products companies for environmentally friendly products growing rapidly, Koskan started his own small company and began researching cost-effective ways of producing polyaspartate for industrial use. Soon, leading chemical companies also began researching the issue, with the consensus being that polyaspartate was the most suitable replacement for polyacrylates. Unfortunately, as with many emerging technologies that lack a supporting infrastructure, polyaspartate’s price was estimated to be four to five times that of the high-volume-production alternative. Given this, the consumer products industry lost interest in the technology, and the chemical industry shelved it. Koskan’s company, however, believing that polyaspartate could nonetheless be market-competitive on its own merits, decided to persevere and focus on specialty application niches. Polyaspartate has since shown unparalleled success at eliminating scale in offshore oil production equipment and is being used by the farming industry to keep chemical fertilizers in the soil longer, reducing pollution of groundwater by the fertilizers. If Koskan’s company can show continued success, it may yet help enliven an environmental chemistry sector saddled with a reputation for ineffectiveness and high cost.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately captures the meaning of the phrase “on its own merits” as it is used in the third-to-last sentence of the passage?

choices.A: without funding from government agencies
choices.B: without reference to its chemical properties
choices.C: once its newest industrial uses are more widely publicized
choices.D: not merely as a general substitute for polyacrylates
choices.E: because of its unsurpassed ability to reduce scale

questions.explanation:
After companies dropped it as a general (cheaper-looking) replacement, Koskan's firm believed it could compete on its own merits in specialty niches, not merely as a polyacrylate substitute.
A — Government funding isn't mentioned.
B — Its chemical properties are exactly its merits.
C — Publicity isn't the point.
E — Its scale-reducing success is one merit, but the phrase contrasts niche value with being a general substitute.

questions.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that the author believes that the failure of leading chemical companies to fully embrace polyaspartate as a replacement for polyacrylates

choices.A: was a result of fears about the potentially harmful consequences to human health of using a new and untested material
choices.B: was not primarily a result of considerations involving costs and profits
choices.C: was not due to a widely accepted belief that polyaspartate is ineffectual
choices.D: was a result of the relative scarcity of the raw material from which polyaspartate is made
choices.E: was due to the belief that consumers would not trust products containing polyaspartate

questions.explanation:
Chemical companies reached a consensus that polyaspartate was "the most suitable replacement," then shelved it over price. So it wasn't shelved for being ineffective.
A — Health fears aren't mentioned.
B — The stated reason is price.
D — Raw-material scarcity isn't mentioned.
E — Consumer trust isn't mentioned.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to

choices.A: describe and analyze one attempt to develop and market a new, promising alternative to an existing product
choices.B: demonstrate the mistakes made in one attempt to develop and market a new, promising alternative to an existing product
choices.C: illustrate the kinds of problems that are likely to be encountered in attempts to market a new, promising alternative to an existing product
choices.D: comment on the state of affairs in an industry that tends to overlook environmentally friendly innovation in favor of maintaining strong profits
choices.E: explain the chemical processes that make a particular new product a promising alternative to an existing product

questions.explanation:
The passage describes one effort (Koskan's) to develop and market polyaspartate and analyzes its obstacles and prospects.
B — The passage presents the persistence positively, not as mistakes.
C — It's about one case, not a typology of problems.
D — The industry is not portrayed as favoring profits over the environment in general.
E — Chemistry is explained briefly, but it isn't the main purpose.
