questions.stem: The passage most strongly suggests that which one of the following is true of both polyaspartate and polyacrylates?

choices.A: They perform identically within any industrial application.
choices.B: They were both discovered as a result of research performed by marine biologists.
choices.C: The chemical industry was aware of their existence long before industrial applications for either one were developed.
choices.D: They both have been used to reduce water pollution.
choices.E: At the time they were first brought to market, leading chemical companies were skeptical about their commercial success.

questions.explanation:
Polyacrylates replaced phosphates that pollute surface waters. Polyaspartate keeps fertilizer in soil, reducing groundwater pollution. Both have been used to reduce water pollution.
A — Polyaspartate is biodegradable and polyacrylates aren't, so not identical.
B — Only polyaspartate's use was inspired by marine biology.
C — Nothing says this.
E — The passage says nothing about skepticism toward polyacrylates.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q1
questions.stimulus: Columnist: The dangers of drinking are greatly exaggerated in the medical press. We are always hearing about the extent to which alcohol can shorten one’s life, but my grandfather drank heavily his entire life and lived to be 95.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the columnist’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.A: does not address moral objections to alcohol consumption
choices.B: fails to consider factors other than alcohol consumption that can shorten one’s life
choices.C: only addresses the length of a life, and not the quality of that life
choices.D: confuses the cause of a phenomenon with an effect of that phenomenon
choices.E: relies merely on anecdotal evidence to challenge a general claim

questions.explanation:
One grandfather who drank heavily and lived to 95 is an anecdote. It can't overturn a general claim about alcohol's effects on lifespan.
A — Morality isn't part of the argument.
B — Other causes of a short life don't bear on the columnist's reasoning.
C — Quality of life is a different issue.
D — No cause and effect are reversed.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q2
questions.stimulus: Some have argued that using food crops to produce fuel represents an unprecedented attack on the food supply. It seems immoral to divert crops from the food supply while there is a need for food. But we currently divert crops from the human food supply to feed livestock. So the diversion of food to fuel is not actually a radical break with traditional practices.
questions.stem: The argument proceeds by

choices.A: arguing that the bad consequences of a practice are outweighed by the good consequences of that practice
choices.B: countering the charge that a practice has a bad consequence by trying to show that the practice does not actually have that consequence
choices.C: rebutting a charge that a practice is radical by contending that the practice is analogous with an existing one
choices.D: rejecting the charge that a practice is immoral by trying to undercut the moral foundation of the charge
choices.E: supporting a moral objection to a practice by trying to show that the practice is actually different from practices that might seem similar

questions.explanation:
The charge is that fuel crops are "unprecedented" (radical). The author replies that we already divert crops to livestock, so it's analogous to an existing practice.
A — No weighing of good and bad consequences.
B — The author doesn't deny the practice reduces food supply; the author denies it's radical.
D — The moral charge is mentioned, but the rebuttal targets "unprecedented," not the moral foundation.
E — The author argues the practices are similar, not different.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q3
questions.stimulus:
Hernandez: Celebrities’ public pronouncements can warp a debate because people grant more weight to celebrities’ opinions than to ordinary people’s. For that reason, celebrities should avoid talking publicly about controversial issues on which they have no expertise.
Liu: But celebrities are full members of their communities. It is not their fault if people give their opinions more credence than they should. So it is absurd that they should not feel free to join controversial debates.
questions.stem: Hernandez and Liu disagree with each other about which one of the following?

choices.A: People grant more weight to celebrities’ opinions than to ordinary people’s.
choices.B: Celebrities should avoid talking publicly about controversial issues on which they have no expertise.
choices.C: Celebrities’ pronouncements on controversial issues can warp debates on those issues.
choices.D: The public should disregard what celebrities say about controversial issues.
choices.E: Celebrities are responsible for the fact that people give their opinions more credence than they should.

questions.explanation:
Hernandez: celebrities should avoid these debates. Liu: it's absurd they shouldn't feel free to join them.
A — Liu seems to accept it ("people give their opinions more credence than they should").
C — Liu doesn't dispute that their remarks can warp debate.
D — Neither says what the public should do.
E — Only Liu addresses fault, and Hernandez never claims celebrities are responsible.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q4
questions.stimulus: A process of extracting caffeine from coffee without seriously compromising the coffee’s taste was introduced a number of years ago. When this decaffeinated coffee first came on the market, however, many coffee drinkers reported that it tasted rather bad.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the statements above?

choices.A: The percentage of coffee drinkers who drink only decaffeinated coffee is much larger today than it was at the time the process was introduced.
choices.B: Many coffee drinkers would not drink decaffeinated coffee even if they believed that it tasted as good as regular coffee.
choices.C: The taste of any kind of coffee can be affected by the foods that are consumed along with it.
choices.D: Coffee that is decaffeinated through this process generally costs more than regular coffee.
choices.E: During the years in which the process was introduced, coffee processors used only low-quality coffee beans for their decaffeinated products.

questions.explanation:
The process didn't hurt taste, but early decaf used low-quality beans. Bad taste came from the beans, not the process.
A — Today's market share doesn't explain the early taste reports.
B — Willingness to drink decaf isn't about taste.
C — Food pairing affects all coffee equally.
D — Price doesn't explain taste.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q5
questions.stimulus: Researchers gave each of eighteen subjects a playing card, then offered them money to lie to a computer about the identity of the card while undergoing a scan by functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). When subjects lied, the scans revealed increased activity in several regions of the brain known to be stimulated by stress. This supports the idea that fMRI can eventually form the basis of an effective lie detector.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would, if true, most weaken the argument above?

choices.A: Existing methods of lie detection, including the polygraph, have not been shown to be reliable.
choices.B: The majority of people regard lying in an experimental situation as unethical.
choices.C: The amount of stress that accompanies lying varies widely from person to person and is also affected by the circumstances in which the lie is told.
choices.D: Telling a carefully planned lie causes less stress than telling a lie spontaneously.
choices.E: Stress reactions in the brains of subjects who are being truthful are similar to those that occur in the brains of subjects who are lying.

questions.explanation:
If truthful subjects show the same stress patterns, the scans can't tell lies from truths, so they can't be the basis of an effective lie detector.
A — Other methods' unreliability doesn't affect fMRI's promise.
B — Ethical views of lying don't affect detection.
C — Variable stress levels complicate things, but the scans could still detect lies if truth-telling showed no such response.
D — Planned lies causing less stress is a limitation, not a basic failure.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q6
questions.stimulus: Prominent government officials have denied that their policies have produced serious environmental degradation. But the facts show otherwise. Last year, at the urging of certain mining companies, the government repealed a long-standing provision prohibiting the dumping of mining wastes into streams. Since that time, hundreds of miles of vital streams have been buried under bulldozed mining wastes.
questions.stem: The argument relies on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.A: Without the urging of certain mining companies, the government would not have lifted the ban on dumping mining wastes into streams.
choices.B: The prominent government officials who deny that government policies have produced serious environmental degradation do not really believe what they are claiming.
choices.C: The mining companies that urged repeal of the ban on dumping mining wastes in streams were among those that buried hundreds of miles of streams under mining wastes.
choices.D: The government is generally more responsive to pressures from the mining industry than from environmentalists.
choices.E: If the ban on dumping mining wastes in streams had not been repealed, considerably less mining waste would have found its way into streams.

questions.explanation:
The argument blames the repeal for buried streams. That requires the repeal to have made a difference: without it, much less waste would have entered streams.
A — Why the government repealed the ban doesn't matter.
B — Officials' sincerity is irrelevant.
C — Which companies dumped doesn't matter; the policy's effect does.
D — A general comparison of lobbying influence is irrelevant.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q7
questions.stimulus: Critic: It generally holds true of concert pianists that the more famous the musician, the greater the pleasure of his or her audience. In my view, this is only fair and should give no cause for cynicism about the ability of audiences to distinguish good playing from bad.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strongly supports the critic’s view?

choices.A: The fame of concert pianists usually reflects their talent as musicians.
choices.B: Some of the finest concert pianists are unknown to the general public.
choices.C: In general, the more famous the pianist, the larger the audiences that he or she can draw.
choices.D: Even the finest concert pianists cannot play consistently well at every performance.
choices.E: The very best concert pianists often perform works that are difficult for audiences to appreciate.

questions.explanation:
The critic says the fame–pleasure link shows audiences can tell good from bad playing. That holds if fame usually reflects talent.
B — Great unknown pianists cut against the idea that fame tracks talent.
C — Audience size isn't about pleasure or discernment.
D — Inconsistent performances don't bear on the critic's view.
E — Suggests the best players may not please audiences most.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q8
questions.stimulus: Scientists found the remains of several species of mites trapped in rocks in a high-altitude cave. Radioactive dating shows that the mites were trapped about 2,000 years ago. The mite species in the rocks no longer live in the vicinity of the cave, but they are found a few miles away in a cooler area. Therefore, the area around the cave was probably cooler 2,000 years ago, since _______.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument is most strongly supported if which one of the following completes the passage?

choices.A: the mite species found in the rocks can only survive in very specific climates
choices.B: the cooler area a few miles away from the cave also has a somewhat wetter climate
choices.C: the mite species that were trapped in the rocks did not live in the vicinity of the cave much earlier than 2,000 years ago
choices.D: the mite species found in the rocks only live at high altitudes
choices.E: there are fewer mite species living in the vicinity of the cave today than there were 2,000 years ago

questions.explanation:
The inference from where the mites live now to past climate needs them to be climate-specific. If they survive only in very specific climates, their presence 2,000 years ago signals a cooler climate then.
B — Wetness is a different variable from coolness.
C — How long they lived there before doesn't bear on climate then.
D — Altitude preference would explain location by height, not temperature, and the cave is already high.
E — Comparing species counts doesn't link these mites to temperature.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q9
questions.stimulus: Market studies confirm that consumers shopping for automobiles primarily seek those that are most reliable. An automobile is reliable if it very rarely breaks down and it does not require significantly more maintenance than average. Strangely enough, however, some of the most reliable models do not sell well with those who say they care most about reliability.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.A: Consumers who are shopping for an automobile claim to care more about reliability than about fuel efficiency.
choices.B: Consumers often choose automobile models based on a reputation for reliability, and reputations can be out of date.
choices.C: Some owners of reliable automobiles are reluctant to trade them in for newer vehicles and tend to hold on to them for the life of the automobile.
choices.D: Some automobile models that have been shown to require a lot of maintenance very rarely break down.
choices.E: Some of the most stylish automobiles are some of the most unreliable.

questions.explanation:
Buyers rely on reputation for reliability, and reputations can lag. A truly reliable model with an outdated poor reputation would sell poorly with reliability-focused buyers.
A — Ranking reliability above fuel efficiency deepens rather than resolves the puzzle.
C — Owners keeping cars doesn't explain why new buyers skip them.
D — About the definition of reliability, not why reliable models don't sell.
E — Unreliable stylish cars don't explain reliable models' weak sales.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q10
questions.stimulus: A recent study found that most individuals believe that they sleep less than most other people. However, it is obviously not possible that most people sleep less than most other people. Therefore, _______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?

choices.A: some people believe things that could not possibly be true even in principle
choices.B: most people are not aware of how much they sleep
choices.C: most people underestimate how much they sleep in comparison to others
choices.D: most people think that they do not sleep as much as they should
choices.E: some people incorrectly believe that they sleep less than most other people

questions.explanation:
Most people can't sleep less than most others, so some of the "most" who believe they do must be wrong.
A — Each individual belief is possible. Only "most are right" is impossible.
B — "Not aware of how much they sleep" goes beyond the data, which is about comparisons.
C — "Most" underestimate isn't guaranteed; only some must be wrong.
D — How much people should sleep isn't discussed.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q11
questions.stimulus: Ross: Many governments have attempted to regulate strictly or even outlaw theater because of its subversive power. Such strategies have rarely succeeded, probably because people strongly desire theater for entertainment and dramatists always find subtle ways to criticize authorities who treat them harshly. Thus, since dramatists will not criticize governments of which they are honored employees, an effective strategy for controlling theater and satisfying the public is to make dramatists and performers honored employees of the government.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken Ross’s argument?

choices.A: Few governments are willing to shoulder the expense of employing dramatists and performers.
choices.B: Even when completely unregulated, theater rarely leads to the overthrow of a government.
choices.C: Some dramatists criticize their governments even though those governments do not treat them harshly.
choices.D: Most theatrical productions neither criticize government nor support it.
choices.E: The public generally dislikes plays written or performed by government employees.

questions.explanation:
Ross's plan must both control theater and satisfy the public. If the public dislikes plays by government employees, the plan fails the second goal.
A — Cost concerns governments' willingness, not whether the strategy would work.
B — Whether theater topples governments isn't Ross's point.
C — Ross's key claim concerns honored employees. Governments merely not treating dramatists harshly is a different case.
D — Most plays being neutral doesn't affect the strategy.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q12
questions.stimulus: Many hikers now carry cell phones so they can call for emergency assistance from remote areas. Many also use their cell phones to call wildlife offices when they see poachers breaking game laws, enabling wildlife agents to reach the scene before the lawbreakers leave. Poachers, however, avoid areas they know to be frequented by hikers.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: Most hikers can afford cell phones.
choices.B: Poaching has decreased as cell phone use has increased.
choices.C: Wildlife agents do not usually carry cell phones.
choices.D: Some hikers hike in areas that are not known by poachers to be frequented by hikers.
choices.E: Cell phones are becoming one of the most effective tools in the effort to protect wildlife from poachers.

questions.explanation:
Hikers do see and report poachers, yet poachers avoid areas known to be frequented by hikers. So some hikers must be in areas poachers don't know hikers frequent.
A — Affordability isn't addressed.
B — No data on poaching trends.
C — Agents' phones aren't discussed.
E — Far too strong.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q13
questions.stimulus: A cognitive psychologist has claimed that intelligence is the ability to figure out how things work in order to overcome obstacles. If, however, we were to become convinced that a particular being had acquired an understanding of how things work, we would certainly not deny that that being possessed intelligence, even if we were sure that its acquisition of this understanding was not prompted by the desire to overcome some specific obstacle. Clearly, then, the cognitive psychologist’s definition is inadequate.
questions.stem: In the passage the author does which one of the following?

choices.A: rejects a definition on the grounds that the terms employed in the definition would make it impractical to determine which cases it covers
choices.B: uses a hypothetical application of a definition to argue that the definition would have unacceptably counterintuitive consequences
choices.C: argues that a proposed definition does not specify the meaning of the concept being defined narrowly enough for the definition to be applied
choices.D: rejects a definition on the grounds that if it were accepted as correct, the term being defined would apply to things to which it normally does not apply
choices.E: argues against a proposed definition on the grounds that those who support it do so at least partly on an inappropriate appeal to authority

questions.explanation:
The author imagines a being that understands how things work without an obstacle motive. We'd call it intelligent, but the definition excludes it. A hypothetical shows the definition gives a counterintuitive result.
A — The issue isn't practicality of applying the terms.
C — The definition is too narrow, not too vague.
D — The author says the definition excludes something it should include (too narrow), not that it includes too much.
E — No appeal to authority is discussed.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q14
questions.stimulus: Environmentalist: The adoption of genetically engineered crops in agriculture is moving so rapidly and is monitored so loosely that it poses a significant risk of damaging sensitive ecosystems. One such crop had already been widely planted when a study found that it could threaten monarch butterflies. Therefore, before any new genetically engineered crop is put into agricultural production, rigorous testing of its safety should be required.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the environmentalist’s reasoning?

choices.A: A genetically engineered crop should not be put into agricultural production if rigorous testing has shown it to be risky.
choices.B: If a crop has no potential for posing environmental risks, it may be put into agricultural production without testing of its safety.
choices.C: No crop that might present risks to the environment should be allowed into agricultural production unless its safety has been thoroughly tested.
choices.D: If rigorous testing of any genetically engineered crop that is in agricultural production shows that that crop poses environmental risks, production of that crop should be discontinued.
choices.E: If rigorous studies do not find evidence that a crop would present risks if it is brought into agricultural production, no further testing of that crop’s safety is required.

questions.explanation:
Conclusion: rigorous testing should be required before any new GE crop goes into production. The principle: no crop that might pose risks is allowed in unless thoroughly tested. GE crops might pose risks, so testing is required.
A — Only says what to do after testing finds risk. Doesn't require testing.
B — Says when testing isn't needed, not that it is needed.
D — About crops already in production.
E — About when further testing isn't required.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q15
questions.stimulus: Faculty member: The university’s financially minded president holds that some academic programs should be eliminated because they do not serve student demands. According to him, the university is a business and the students are consumers, and it is the responsibility of any business to satisfy consumer demand. But the education of students is not analogous to the providing of consumer goods. Therefore, the president is mistaken in claiming that academic programs should be tailored to suit student demand.
questions.stem: The faculty member’s argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that it

choices.A: argues for a view without showing that an argument against that view fails
choices.B: appeals to popular opinion to justify a conclusion
choices.C: treats merely analogous things as identical
choices.D: improperly attacks the university president’s moral character
choices.E: rejects a view on the grounds that someone has given inadequate reasons for accepting that view

questions.explanation:
The faculty member shows the president's analogy fails, then concludes the president's claim is false. A bad reason for a claim doesn't make the claim false.
A — Sounds close, but the faculty member attacks the president's argument rather than ignoring it. The flaw is concluding falsity from it.
B — No appeal to popular opinion.
C — The faculty member denies the analogy; the president is the one treating them alike.
D — No attack on character.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q16
questions.stimulus: A recent study carefully tracked the specific behaviors of five East African chimpanzee groups of one subspecies, and of two West African groups of another subspecies, in activities such as grooming and foraging. The study found that one of the East African groups was behaviorally more similar to the West African groups than to the other East African groups. It is therefore likely that these behaviors are determined by cultural factors rather than by genetics.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, provides the most support for the argument?

choices.A: Chimpanzees sometimes copy the behavior of other chimpanzees, whether or not they are closely related genetically.
choices.B: Chimpanzees that are new to a group sometimes bring with them new behaviors as well as new genetic characteristics.
choices.C: The chimpanzee groups studied face different environmental challenges due to their different locations in Africa.
choices.D: The behavioral differences in the chimpanzee groups studied are sufficient to make each group recognizably distinct from all the others.
choices.E: Of the chimpanzee groups studied, the five East African groups live in closer proximity to each other than do the two West African groups.

questions.explanation:
Behavior crosses subspecies lines, which suggests it isn't genetic. If chimps copy behaviors regardless of relatedness, cultural transmission is a mechanism that explains the pattern.
B — New members bring genes as well as behaviors, so genetics could still explain it.
C — Environment offers an alternative to culture.
D — Distinctness doesn't bear on the cause.
E — If East African groups are closer, culture should make them more alike, so the odd group is harder to explain culturally.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q17
questions.stimulus: Essayist: It would be wrong to defend current testing procedures for new medications simply by appealing to the fact that test subjects are volunteers who are both apprised of and compensated for the risks involved. For while it is not wrong to pay people to do something if they are freely choosing to do it, the same cannot be said if the choice is made under duress.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the essayist’s argument?

choices.A: Possessing information about the possible consequences of the choices one makes does not ensure that one’s choices are free.
choices.B: No transaction can be justified merely on the grounds that those participating in the transaction do so voluntarily.
choices.C: Anyone who acts without complete freedom is acting under some form of externally imposed duress.
choices.D: There is nothing wrong with accepting money for putting oneself at risk.
choices.E: People should be permitted to perform any action so long as that action is freely chosen.

questions.explanation:
Defenders point to subjects being informed and paid. The essayist says that's not enough because choices could be under duress. That assumes being informed doesn't ensure a free choice.
B — "No transaction" overreaches. The essayist's point is narrower.
C — What counts as duress beyond lack of freedom isn't needed.
D — The essayist allows payment for free choices but doesn't need this broader claim.
E — Permission for any free action isn't required.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q18
questions.stimulus: Putting a tap in a healthy maple that has a trunk 12 or more inches in diameter will not harm the tree. Silver maples, red maples, and Manitoba maples can all be tapped for making maple syrup. The sugar maple, however, is best for syrup making, because of all the maples its sap has the highest concentration of sugar.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: A maple whose trunk is more than 12 inches in diameter is unhealthy if it is harmed by tapping.
choices.B: The healthiest maple trees are usually those with the largest trunks.
choices.C: A maple tree that has been harmed will produce very little sap.
choices.D: Putting a tap into an unhealthy maple tree that is less than 12 inches in diameter will harm it.
choices.E: The maple trees most commonly used for making syrup are sugar maples.

questions.explanation:
Healthy and at least 12 inches → not harmed by tapping. So a 12-plus-inch maple harmed by tapping must be unhealthy.
B — Nothing relates trunk size to health.
C — Sap production isn't discussed.
D — The statement says nothing about unhealthy or small trees. That negates the condition.
E — "Best for syrup" doesn't mean most commonly used.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q19
questions.stimulus: Company spokesperson: Although our products are the most expensive in our industry, they are also the best available. After all, consider any less expensive product made by one of our competitors. If it were as good as, or better than, our product, it would cost as much, or more.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the company spokesperson’s argument is flawed in that the argument

choices.A: contains a premise that presupposes the truth of the conclusion
choices.B: fails to make a needed distinction between the best product currently available and the best product that could be produced
choices.C: treats a cause of a product being the most expensive as an effect of its being the most expensive
choices.D: presumes that because something is true of each of a company’s products it is also true of the company as a whole
choices.E: bases a conclusion on claims that are inconsistent with each other

questions.explanation:
"If a cheaper product were as good, it would cost as much" already assumes price tracks quality, which is the point at issue.
B — Possible products aren't relevant.
C — No causal reversal.
D — No part-to-whole move.
E — The claims are consistent, just circular.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q20
questions.stimulus: It should be illegal to patent an organism’s genes, for a person should not be regarded as the inventor of something he or she merely discovered. Moreover, exploitation of genetic information for profit is selfish and irresponsible.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the argument?

choices.A: Any person who exploits genetic information for profit should be considered selfish.
choices.B: Discovering something should not entitle one to patent it.
choices.C: Discovering something does not always constitute inventing it.
choices.D: No person should be allowed to profit from something that was invented by another person.
choices.E: A person or corporation who invents something should be entitled to patent it.

questions.explanation:
The core reasoning: genes are discovered, not invented, so they shouldn't be patentable. The principle "discovering shouldn't entitle one to a patent" makes that work.
A — Supports only the side remark about selfishness, not illegality of patents.
C — Distinguishes discovery from invention but doesn't connect to patent rights.
D — Profiting from others' inventions isn't the issue.
E — Invention → patent doesn't imply discovery → no patent.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q21
questions.stimulus: Professor O’Brien: Any of my students who heard Mercado’s lecture from the beginning would have thought it was fascinating, and I know that some of my students did think it was fascinating, so some of my students must have heard it from the beginning.
questions.stem: Professor O’Brien’s argument does not follow logically from its premises because of the possibility that

choices.A: some of Professor O’Brien’s students are very interested in Mercado’s work but were unable to attend the lecture
choices.B: many people who are not Professor O’Brien’s students did not think that the lecture was fascinating, even though they heard it from the beginning
choices.C: some of Professor O’Brien’s students were a few minutes late for the lecture and did not find the lecture fascinating
choices.D: no one who heard the lecture from the beginning and thought that it was fascinating was one of Professor O’Brien’s students
choices.E: not everyone who arrived at the lecture on time was able to hear the entire lecture because of disruptions caused by those who were late in arriving

questions.explanation:
Heard from the beginning → found it fascinating. Some students found it fascinating, therefore some heard from the beginning: affirming the consequent. If none of the fascinated beginning-listeners were his students (his fascinated students arrived late), the premises hold and the conclusion fails.
A — Students who didn't attend don't matter.
B — Non-students are irrelevant.
C — Late students who weren't fascinated don't threaten the inference.
E — Disruptions don't address the logical gap.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q22
questions.stimulus: Some moral virtues, such as honesty, tend to benefit one who has them; others, such as generosity, do not. A personal characteristic is not a moral virtue if it tends to be detrimental to other people.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: A person totally lacking in moral virtue will tend not to have characteristics that benefit others.
choices.B: Being honest tends not to be detrimental to other people.
choices.C: A morally virtuous person tends to be a greater benefit to other people than a person who is not morally virtuous.
choices.D: Being generous tends to be to one’s own detriment but not to the detriment of others.
choices.E: If a personal characteristic that one has tends to benefit others, then that personal characteristic is a moral virtue.

questions.explanation:
Honesty is a moral virtue. No virtue tends to harm others. So honesty tends not to harm others.
A — Nothing says non-virtues can't benefit others.
C — Comparative benefit isn't established.
D — Generosity "does not" benefit oneself, which isn't the same as harming oneself.
E — Benefit to others → virtue reverses nothing stated and isn't implied.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q23
questions.stimulus: During last year’s flu season no one who was vaccinated contracted the flu. This year every student at South High School has been vaccinated. So this flu season none of the students at South High School will contract the flu.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.A: No camper who used insect repellent last month was disturbed by mosquitoes. Since everyone in our campsite has applied insect repellent tonight, none of us will be disturbed by mosquitoes tonight.
choices.B: Last year, Marie purchased a car that had been well maintained. Since Marie will certainly continue to maintain the car this year, the car is unlikely to have mechanical problems this year.
choices.C: Last year, no student with perfect attendance failed a class, and all students in advanced history had perfect attendance. So no student in advanced history last year failed the class.
choices.D: All the fruit we purchased yesterday was fresh. All the fruit we bought yesterday is in the refrigerator. Therefore, all the fruit in the refrigerator is fresh.
choices.E: No sparrow eats seeds with hard shells. All seeds of this tree have hard shells. So no sparrow will eat the seeds of this tree.

questions.explanation:
Original: last season, no vaccinated person got the flu; this year all of a group is vaccinated; so none will get it. Camping: last month, repellent users weren't bothered; tonight all applied it; so none will be bothered.
B — One car, a "likely" conclusion, and no prior-group generalization.
C — Applies last year's fact to last year's group. A valid deduction, not a projection to a new time.
D — A valid syllogism with no projection forward.
E — A timeless generalization, not "last period → this period."

traps.B: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q24
questions.stimulus: Advertising agencies are often wrongly criticized for causing people to desire, and thus purchase, products they do not really need. People actually buy what they buy mainly because they believe the product will satisfy their desires—a belief that, admittedly, it is the purpose of advertising agencies to induce. It is clear then that the desires that people believe products will satisfy _______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?

choices.A: can be classified as needs if they actually prompt people to make a purchase
choices.B: are created by false, but not by true, advertising claims
choices.C: will rarely be satisfied by the purchases they prompt
choices.D: are exploited rather than created by advertisers
choices.E: are generally what induce people to believe claims made by advertisers

questions.explanation:
Ads don't create desires; they induce beliefs that products will satisfy existing desires. So advertisers exploit desires rather than create them.
A — Needs versus desires isn't resolved by purchases.
B — True versus false claims aren't discussed.
C — Whether purchases satisfy desires isn't addressed.
E — The argument says ads induce beliefs, not that desires induce belief in ads.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q25
questions.stimulus: Artist: I have never won a prize at the Art Competition, even though several of my submitted paintings have received widespread recognition and have sold thousands of copies as posters. I know six other popular artists who have submitted works to that competition and fared no better. Thus, winning the Art Competition proves that an artist is no good.
questions.stem: The pattern of flawed reasoning in which one of the following arguments most closely resembles that in the artist’s argument?

choices.A: Researcher: I have never won a prize at the Science Competition, although I have obtained patents for several of my inventions and they have been extremely lucrative. Other scientists have had similar experiences. Therefore, the judges are using some criterion other than marketability to judge the inventions.
choices.B: Cook: I always win a prize at the Cooking Competition, even though my entries are regarded by the general public as unusual and unappealing. Other cooks have reported similar experiences. Thus, winning proves that one’s culinary creation is not to most people’s taste.
choices.C: Professor: The same essays that have won nothing in some years at the Philosophical Essay Competition have won the grand prize in other years. So the essays are not judged entirely on quality.
choices.D: Student: The student government never takes my proposals seriously, even when these proposals have the support of most students. Others have also introduced widely supported proposals, but the student government has not seriously considered theirs either. So the student government takes only bad proposals seriously.
choices.E: Travel agent: When I do my most creative and dedicated work, the airlines reduce my commissions. And when I do rushed work, they send me fruit baskets in gratitude. I conclude that airlines want to discourage good ideas and hard work.

questions.explanation:
The artist: good, popular work doesn't win, so winning shows an artist is bad. From "good things don't get the reward" to "only bad things get it." The student's argument does the same.
A — Concludes the judges use some other criterion, which is a reasonable inference.
B — Based on the arguer winning, a different structure.
C — Infers inconsistent judging, a reasonable conclusion.
E — Infers motives from rewards and penalties, close but drawn from a pattern of responses rather than from good entries never winning.

traps.B: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure
traps.C: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 3 (Reading Comprehension), Q1
questions.stimulus:
The 1937–1938 comic strip Torchy Brown, in “Dixie to Harlem” by Jackie Ormes would have been distinctive if only for its heritage—it was almost certainly the first strip to be written and drawn by an African American woman. In 53 weekly episodes, Ormes sketched the experiences of a glamorous heroine who moves from her home in the South to a new life and career at New York’s famed Cotton Club.
At first glance, Torchy’s adventures might seem as incredible as a fairy tale. The opening panels present a rural Southern community that is nearly idyllic, as Torchy is cared for by a loving aunt and uncle, and freely moves through a pastoral terrain. While journeying to the North, the character is, in the best fairy tale tradition, beleaguered by ominous predators and aided by mysterious helpers. Once in New York, she instantly achieves success as a performer at the Cotton Club, where she mingles comfortably with such African American musical legends as Duke Ellington and Cab Calloway.
Despite the strip’s gestures in the direction of the fantastic, Torchy Brown clearly reflects significant cultural concerns. Through her exploration of an entertainer’s lifestyle in the almost mythic setting of the Cotton Club, Ormes celebrated and amplified the success of real African Americans who had achieved wide respect for their skill as hardworking and talented professionals. Indeed, so many sequences take place in or around the Cotton Club with Torchy in rehearsal or performance that the Club becomes a symbol for a place where African Americans are measured by what they have to offer, where they are looked upon by a white audience as admirable, instead of being overlooked or looked through. In several episodes, moreover, Ormes explicitly and provocatively likened the artistry of improvisation found in swing music and tap dance with the form of her own comic strip. In the process, Ormes left a record of a moment in the evolution of jazz that also aligned the comic strip, as a mass culture form, with another popular art.
Ormes clearly enjoyed Torchy’s triumphs at the Cotton Club, which mirrored her own success as a cartoonist, but she never shied away from the darker possibilities that made Torchy’s victories so important. Even during Torchy’s “fantastic” journey to New York, the all-too-real world of segregation laws intrudes when Torchy must decide which train car to board. Ormes knew how quickly a newcomer can misread signs and fall into danger. By placing her character in authentic situations where much depends on the courage of the individual, she expanded her social commentary to offer real-life lessons for her audience.
questions.stem: The passage is primarily concerned with

choices.A: discussing the influence and legacy of a little-known cartoonist
choices.B: exploring a moment in the evolution of jazz as recorded in a comic strip
choices.C: comparing the techniques of a cartoonist’s art with the improvisational methods of jazz
choices.D: showing how the narrative of one comic strip bears a resemblance to the genre of fairy tales
choices.E: analyzing the significance of a comic strip that was unusual because of both its author and its themes

questions.explanation:
The passage notes the strip's unusual heritage (first by an African American woman), then analyzes its fairy-tale surface, cultural concerns, and social commentary.
A — Influence and legacy aren't discussed, and Ormes isn't framed as little-known.
B — Jazz comes up in one paragraph only.
C — The jazz comparison is one detail.
D — The fairy-tale resemblance is set up only to be qualified.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly suggested by the passage?

choices.A: Torchy Brown might have achieved greater popular success if it had not tackled troubling social issues such as segregation laws.
choices.B: The value of Torchy Brown as a work of art is diminished by its heavy emphasis on fantastic elements.
choices.C: Popular comic strips often make use of the fairy tale tradition of storytelling.
choices.D: Music was a cultural arena in which African American artists in the 1920s and 1930s enjoyed success and wide recognition of their talents.
choices.E: The African American migration from the South to the North in the 1920s and 1930s was documented in numerous works of popular art from the period.

questions.explanation:
Ormes "celebrated and amplified the success of real African Americans," with Torchy mingling with Ellington and Calloway, who were widely respected. Music was an arena of recognized achievement.
A — Nothing suggests social issues hurt the strip's popularity.
B — The author values its cultural concerns, and the fantasy elements are framed neutrally.
C — Nothing about comic strips in general.
E — "Numerous works" isn't supported.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Ormes likened the form of her comic strip to the artistry of which one of the following?

choices.A: fairy tales
choices.B: tap dance
choices.C: poetry
choices.D: painting
choices.E: acting

questions.stem: Which one of the following aspects of Torchy Brown does the author of the passage appear to value most highly?

choices.A: its idyllic portrayal of the rural South in the 1920s and 1930s
choices.B: its focus on music and dance as symbolic of African American achievement
choices.C: its glamorous heroine, whose exciting experiences provided entertainment for Ormes’s readers

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 3 (Reading Comprehension), Q5
questions.stimulus:
The 1937–1938 comic strip Torchy Brown, in “Dixie to Harlem” by Jackie Ormes would have been distinctive if only for its heritage—it was almost certainly the first strip to be written and drawn by an African American woman. In 53 weekly episodes, Ormes sketched the experiences of a glamorous heroine who moves from her home in the South to a new life and career at New York’s famed Cotton Club.
At first glance, Torchy’s adventures might seem as incredible as a fairy tale. The opening panels present a rural Southern community that is nearly idyllic, as Torchy is cared for by a loving aunt and uncle, and freely moves through a pastoral terrain. While journeying to the North, the character is, in the best fairy tale tradition, beleaguered by ominous predators and aided by mysterious helpers. Once in New York, she instantly achieves success as a performer at the Cotton Club, where she mingles comfortably with such African American musical legends as Duke Ellington and Cab Calloway.
Despite the strip’s gestures in the direction of the fantastic, Torchy Brown clearly reflects significant cultural concerns. Through her exploration of an entertainer’s lifestyle in the almost mythic setting of the Cotton Club, Ormes celebrated and amplified the success of real African Americans who had achieved wide respect for their skill as hardworking and talented professionals. Indeed, so many sequences take place in or around the Cotton Club with Torchy in rehearsal or performance that the Club becomes a symbol for a place where African Americans are measured by what they have to offer, where they are looked upon by a white audience as admirable, instead of being overlooked or looked through. In several episodes, moreover, Ormes explicitly and provocatively likened the artistry of improvisation found in swing music and tap dance with the form of her own comic strip. In the process, Ormes left a record of a moment in the evolution of jazz that also aligned the comic strip, as a mass culture form, with another popular art.
Ormes clearly enjoyed Torchy’s triumphs at the Cotton Club, which mirrored her own success as a cartoonist, but she never shied away from the darker possibilities that made Torchy’s victories so important. Even during Torchy’s “fantastic” journey to New York, the all-too-real world of segregation laws intrudes when Torchy must decide which train car to board. Ormes knew how quickly a newcomer can misread signs and fall into danger. By placing her character in authentic situations where much depends on the courage of the individual, she expanded her social commentary to offer real-life lessons for her audience.
questions.stem: The author cites each of the following as a fairy-tale-like element of Torchy Brown except:

choices.A: instant success
choices.B: magical symbols
choices.C: mysterious helpers
choices.D: ominous predators
choices.E: pastoral terrain

questions.explanation:
The passage cites pastoral terrain, ominous predators, mysterious helpers, and instant success as fairy-tale elements. Magical symbols are never mentioned.
A — Cited: "she instantly achieves success."
C — Cited: "aided by mysterious helpers."
D — Cited: "beleaguered by ominous predators."
E — Cited: "freely moves through a pastoral terrain."

questions.stem: The passage most strongly suggests that Ormes would agree with which one of the following statements about her character, Torchy Brown?

choices.A: She personified the complexity of the traditional fairy tale heroine.
choices.B: Her options were severely limited by her time and place.
choices.C: She was courageous and could serve as a role model for the audience.
choices.D: Her life as a performer was shaped by her struggle to achieve artistic recognition.
choices.E: Her experiences were important precisely because they were so improbable.

questions.explanation:
Ormes placed Torchy "in authentic situations where much depends on the courage of the individual... to offer real-life lessons for her audience." Courage and role-model status follow.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 3 (Reading Comprehension), Q7
questions.stimulus:
The following two passages were adapted from articles published in 2005 and 2002, respectively.
Passage A
There have been two notable efforts to supply credit to self-employed poor people in developing countries. One has been the creation by developing-country governments of state banks, particularly to provide financing to the rural poor. These have mostly been a disaster. The other, much more successful effort involved a number of organizations extending uncollateralized loans to very poor borrowers. One such organization, Bangladesh’s Grameen Bank, started in 1976 and soon became famous for its “microcredit” business model.
To qualify, Grameen’s customers had to be extremely poor, typically earning less than a dollar a day. To overcome the lack of collateral or data about creditworthiness, customers were required to join small groups whose members monitor each other at weekly meetings, applying varying degrees of pressure to ensure repayment. As loans were repaid, people were allowed to borrow more. The group replaced the security that collateral provides. The model is not perfect, but it does have real virtues and has since spread around the world.
Why did microfinance organizations like Grameen originally limit themselves to providing credit? They assumed that poor people were unable to save and that their sole need was for capital. This assumption, however, was probably faulty at the outset. When BRI, a failing state-controlled rural lender in Indonesia, was transformed into a bank serving poor customers in 1984, it offered not only the usual loan products but also a government-guaranteed savings account with no minimum deposit. This has been an extraordinary success: BRI now has 30 million savings accounts.
Passage B
SafeSave is a financial services provider operating in the slums of Dhaka, Bangladesh. With fewer than 5,500 clients, SafeSave is still a small organization, but it is attracting attention because of its unique products. These products are designed to enable very poor urban residents to turn their capacity to save into usefully large lump sums as conveniently and in as many ways as possible.
In essence, SafeSave offers its clients a full banking service on their doorstep, without asking them to form groups. Bank workers, called collectors, visit each client every day, six days a week. On each visit clients may save, or withdraw, or repay loans in any amount they choose. They may also take loans on their doorstep in values based on their proven capacity to save and repay. Given this flexibility, many clients transact very regularly, in volumes that exceed those of more conventional schemes for poor people. This helps explain why SafeSave’s clients tend to pay back loans more quickly than do those of Grameen Bank.
The low interest rate it charges for loans is enough to cover SafeSave’s operational costs, in part because of cost-cutting devices such as recruiting collectors from among the urban poor themselves, and full computerization. With growth, SafeSave promises to become fully economically sustainable.
questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with

choices.A: arguing that financial services providers for poor people in developing countries should offer more than just loans
choices.B: describing successful approaches to providing financial services to poor people in developing countries
choices.C: exploring the roles that can be played by microfinance organizations in improving employment opportunities for poor people in developing countries
choices.D: comparing successful and unsuccessful approaches to supplying credit to self-employed poor people in developing countries
choices.E: demonstrating that microfinance organizations can both do good work and be economically sustainable

questions.explanation:
A describes Grameen's microcredit and BRI's savings success. B describes SafeSave's doorstep services. Both describe successful approaches.
A — A implies this; B doesn't argue it.
C — Employment opportunities aren't discussed.
D — Only A mentions unsuccessful state banks.
E — Sustainability comes up only in B.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is mentioned in passage B but not in passage A?

choices.A: a way in which a financial services provider minimizes the costs involved in doing business
choices.B: the demand for savings accounts among poor people in developing countries
choices.C: ways in which private financial services providers compare favorably with state-controlled providers
choices.D: the competitive advantage enjoyed by microfinance organizations that offer savings accounts as well as providing credit
choices.E: means by which a financial services provider can motivate customers to repay their loans on time

questions.stem: By describing BRI as having been a “failing state-controlled rural lender” (middle of the third paragraph), the author of passage A does which one of the following?

choices.A: deliberately contrasts BRI’s organizational history with the organizational histories of Grameen Bank and SafeSave
choices.B: supports the contention in passage A that it is particularly difficult to provide financial services to poor people in rural areas
choices.C: provides the basis of an explanation of why BRI offers savings accounts in addition to loan products
choices.D: counters the view implied in passage B that microcredit institutions will not be successful if they are not built at the grassroots level
choices.E: identifies BRI as emerging out of what passage A elsewhere characterizes as an unsuccessful approach to providing financial services to poor people

questions.explanation:
A calls state banks "mostly a disaster." Calling BRI a failing state lender shows it emerged from that unsuccessful approach before being transformed.
A — A doesn't mention SafeSave.
B — Rural difficulty isn't argued.
C — Its failing status doesn't explain the savings accounts.
D — Neither passage claims grassroots origins are necessary.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would pose the most serious challenge to the explanation offered in the last two sentences of the second paragraph of passage B?

choices.A: SafeSave generally extends its clients larger loans than Grameen Bank does.
choices.B: SafeSave has far fewer clients than more established microfinance organizations such as Grameen Bank have.
choices.C: Urban poor people in Bangladesh generally borrow larger amounts than do rural poor people.
choices.D: The customers that SafeSave takes on tend to be financially better off than those that Grameen Bank takes on.
choices.E: Loan repayment rates at most banks in Bangladesh are higher than those at either SafeSave or Grameen Bank.

questions.explanation:

B — Client numbers don't explain repayment speed.
C — Urban versus rural borrowing size doesn't challenge the explanation.
E — Other banks' rates don't undercut the SafeSave–Grameen comparison.

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements is most strongly supported by both passages?

choices.A: To be economically sustainable, a financial services provider serving poor people must offer unique products.
choices.B: Holding collateral is the most effective means of ensuring the repayment of loans.
choices.C: There is significant demand for savings accounts among poor people in developing countries.
choices.D: A microfinance organization should be economically sustainable but should not make a profit.
choices.E: Microfinance organizations tend to have more success among urban poor people than among rural poor people.

questions.explanation:
A: BRI's savings accounts are an "extraordinary success" (30 million accounts). B: SafeSave is built around poor clients' capacity to save. Both show demand.
A — Neither says unique products are necessary.
B — A says groups replaced collateral; neither ranks collateral as most effective.
D — Profit isn't discussed this way.
E — Neither compares urban and rural success.

questions.stem: The authors of the passages would be most likely to agree that microfinance organizations

choices.A: must remain small operations if they are to be viable over the long term

choices.C: contribute to economic progress among poor people in developing countries

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of passage A?

choices.A: Microfinance organizations like Grameen Bank are in decline because they failed to fully understand the financial needs of their customer base.
choices.B: Bangladesh’s Grameen Bank developed an innovative business model that has been emulated by financial services providers around the world.

D — Just the first paragraph's contrast.

There have been two notable efforts to supply credit to self-employed poor people in developing countries. One has been the creation by developing-country governments of state banks, particularly to provide financing to the rural poor. These have mostly been a disaster. The other, much more successful effort involved a number of organizations extending uncollateralized loans to very poor borrowers. One such organization, Bangladesh’s Grameen Bank, started in 1976 and soon became famous for its “microcredit” business model.
To qualify, Grameen’s customers had to be extremely poor, typically earning less than a dollar a day. To overcome the lack of collateral or data about creditworthiness, customers were required to join small groups whose members monitor each other at weekly meetings, applying varying degrees of pressure to ensure repayment. As loans were repaid, people were allowed to borrow more. The group replaced the security that collateral provides. The model is not perfect, but it does have real virtues and has since spread around the world.
Why did microfinance organizations like Grameen originally limit themselves to providing credit? They assumed that poor people were unable to save and that their sole need was for capital. This assumption, however, was probably faulty at the outset. When BRI, a failing state-controlled rural lender in Indonesia, was transformed into a bank serving poor customers in 1984, it offered not only the usual loan products but also a government-guaranteed savings account with no minimum deposit. This has been an extraordinary success: BRI now has 30 million savings accounts.
Passage B
SafeSave is a financial services provider operating in the slums of Dhaka, Bangladesh. With fewer than 5,500 clients, SafeSave is still a small organization, but it is attracting attention because of its unique products. These products are designed to enable very poor urban residents to turn their capacity to save into usefully large lump sums as conveniently and in as many ways as possible.
In essence, SafeSave offers its clients a full banking service on their doorstep, without asking them to form groups. Bank workers, called collectors, visit each client every day, six days a week. On each visit clients may save, or withdraw, or repay loans in any amount they choose. They may also take loans on their doorstep in values based on their proven capacity to save and repay. Given this flexibility, many clients transact very regularly, in volumes that exceed those of more conventional schemes for poor people. This helps explain why SafeSave’s clients tend to pay back loans more quickly than do those of Grameen Bank.
The low interest rate it charges for loans is enough to cover SafeSave’s operational costs, in part because of cost-cutting devices such as recruiting collectors from among the urban poor themselves, and full computerization. With growth, SafeSave promises to become fully economically sustainable.
questions.stem: The relationship between Grameen’s business model and those of BRI and SafeSave is most analogous to the relationship between

choices.A: an inspiring teacher and the students who carry the teacher’s lessons to new audiences
choices.B: a highly original architect and the engineers who find practical, new means of implementing the architect’s ideas
choices.C: a successful, classic version of a device and competing versions that incorporate a new component that improves overall performance
choices.D: a mayor who implemented a successful program in one city and mayors elsewhere who adapted that program to make it work in their cities
choices.E: a simple, inexpensive product intended for low-income buyers and upgraded varieties of that product intended for wealthier buyers

questions.explanation:
Grameen is the famous classic model. BRI and SafeSave offer added features (savings, flexible doorstep service) that improve outcomes, like rival versions adding a component.
A — BRI and SafeSave aren't presented as Grameen's disciples spreading its lessons.
B — Nothing suggests they implement Grameen's ideas.
D — They aren't adaptations of Grameen's program; they offer different products.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 3 (Reading Comprehension), Q15
questions.stimulus:
Since 1929, cosmologists have known that the universe is expanding. Until recently, they assumed that the expansion is slowing as the universe’s own gravity tugs against it. In the late 1990s, astronomers set out to observe the slowing by measuring the distances to exploding stars known as supernovas. To their surprise, the farthest supernovas were much more distant than expected. These findings meant that the expansion of the universe is actually accelerating.
Cosmologists have proposed two explanations for the accelerated expansion of the universe, each one a challenge to the current conception of the universe. The first and more widely accepted theory posits a kind of “dark energy” that causes space itself to stretch. Recent studies of the afterglow of the big bang have bolstered the case for dark energy, suggesting that it might even account for a whopping two thirds of the universe’s contents. The simplest version of the dark energy theory postulates that dark energy is an inherent part of the vacuum of space, and that it exerts a constant pressure. The basic notion dates back to 1917, when Einstein proposed such a quantity of pressure, which he labeled the “cosmological constant,” in order to explain why the universe is not shrinking under its own gravity. He later abandoned the notion as unnecessary when astronomers found that the universe is in fact expanding, but Einstein’s orphaned idea may in fact point to what drives the acceleration.
Some cosmologists postulate that the dark energy that drives the accelerated expansion of the universe is created by a class of “virtual” particles. Particle physicists have known for many decades that, thanks to quantum mechanics, the so-called “vacuum” roils with virtual subatomic particles popping in and out of existence, a process that generates a constant vacuum energy. According to the dark energy theorists, this vacuum energy constitutes the dark energy on which their theory depends. Unfortunately, however, there is a large discrepancy between the predicted value of the vacuum energy and the amount of energy needed to explain the accelerated expansion.
This discrepancy is not an issue for the second theory, as it does not invoke the concept of dark energy at all. Instead, it explains the accelerated expansion of the universe by positing that across very large distances—billions of light-years—gravity no longer works as Einstein’s general theory of relativity predicts. Such a change to the theory of gravity would be quite radical, and it would presumably have significant implications for the way gravity works even at short distances. Because these implications could be tested in our own solar system, this might actually be an advantage for the radical theory, since it means that this theory may be easier to test than the dark energy theory.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the central idea of the passage?

choices.A: Researchers hypothesize the existence of dark energy to explain the unexpected accelerated expansion of the universe.
choices.B: Though there is good observational evidence for the accelerated expansion of the universe, there is thus far little evidence for dark energy itself.
choices.C: The current proposals about the nature of dark energy entail that Einstein’s general theory of relativity is incomplete or flawed in some manner.
choices.D: Scientists have proposed two explanations of the accelerated expansion of the universe, but neither fits perfectly with accepted science.
choices.E: The best explanation of the accelerated expansion of the universe is one that rejects the notion of dark energy.

questions.explanation:
Two explanations of acceleration are offered, and each challenges current understanding: dark energy has a discrepancy problem, and modified gravity is radical.
A — Covers only the first theory.
B — The passage notes evidence that has "bolstered the case for dark energy."
C — Only the second theory modifies general relativity.
E — The author notes the second theory may be easier to test, not that it's best.

questions.location: February 2024 LSAT Disclosure, Section 3 (Reading Comprehension), Q22
questions.stimulus:
For most of the past century, scholars in the Anglo-American legal tradition have been skeptical of the view that legal ownership is a matter of possessing any single right. They have advocated the view that ownership is a “bundle of rights” arising from individual judicial decisions in widely diverse cases (e.g., the rights to lease, sell, subdivide, and tax). Accordingly, the concept of ownership per se does not constrain judges’ decisions in the resolution of conflicts regarding property use, since the set of rights corresponding to ownership is itself a product of earlier judicial decisions and is open ended. This theory has been criticized by recent proponents of an older view— that ownership is a basic right to exclude others from a particular thing. According to this “boundary theory,” appealing, in judicial reasoning, to the right to exclude others is by definition equivalent to appealing to ownership, and so the concept of ownership constrains judicial reasoning.
But while the boundary theory properly recognizes that there is a concept of ownership that constrains legal decisions, it fails to explain crucial features of ownership. Indeed, we might better characterize the view as a theory of nonownership. Its focus is on the position of nonowners, defined in terms of a general duty not to cross the boundaries of objects one does not own. The boundary theory, in effect, relies on a process of elimination to distinguish owners from nonowners: an owner is the last person left after the exclusion of everyone else from the object owned. But this provides only the weakest possible account of the owner’s special position: by default the owner is the only one at liberty to use the object after the exclusion of others.
While there is a grain of truth in the boundary theory inasmuch as ownership is an exclusive right, the boundary theory wrongly assumes that what it means for ownership to be exclusive is just that others generally have a duty to exclude themselves from the object owned. However, there is a distinction between a right’s being exclusive in the sense that it excludes others from the object of the right and its being exclusive in the sense that its holder occupies a special position that others do not share. A third theory, the “agenda-setting theory,” regards ownership as an exclusive right in the second sense but not the first. What it means for ownership to be exclusive is that owners are in a special position to set the agenda for a resource (e.g., farm owners determining the specific uses of their land). The law preserves the exclusivity of ownership not by excluding others, but by harmonizing their interests with the owner’s agenda-setting authority. This, rather than the boundary theory’s “exclusivity,” is the essence of ownership.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.A: The bundle-of-rights theory of legal ownership is flawed because it fails to recognize the proper role of ownership in judicial reasoning.
choices.B: The bundle-of-rights theory views legal ownership as a group of diverse rights, whereas the boundary and agenda-setting theories view legal ownership as a single right.
choices.C: The agenda-setting theory more adequately captures the essence of legal ownership than does either the bundle-of-rights theory or the boundary theory.
choices.D: The boundary theory of legal ownership, while superior to the bundle-of-rights theory, fails to definitively distinguish between owners and nonowners.
choices.E: The agenda-setting theory of legal ownership is superior to the boundary theory because the agenda-setting theory focuses solely on excluding others from the owned thing.

questions.explanation:
The author critiques bundle-of-rights and boundary theories and concludes the agenda-setting theory captures "the essence of ownership."
A — Only the boundary theory's critique of bundle theory.
B — A contrast in the passage, but not its main point.
D — The author's main complaint is that the boundary theory gives the weakest account of the owner's position, and the main point is broader.
E — The agenda-setting theory explicitly isn't about excluding others.

This theory has been criticized by recent proponents of an older view— that ownership is a basic right to exclude others from a particular thing. According to this “boundary theory,” appealing, in judicial reasoning, to the right to exclude others is by definition equivalent to appealing to ownership, and so the concept of ownership constrains judicial reasoning.
But while the boundary theory properly recognizes that there is a concept of ownership that constrains legal decisions, it fails to explain crucial features of ownership. Indeed, we might better characterize the view as a theory of nonownership. Its focus is on the position of nonowners, defined in terms of a general duty not to cross the boundaries of objects one does not own. The boundary theory, in effect, relies on a process of elimination to distinguish owners from nonowners: an owner is the last person left after the exclusion of everyone else from the object owned. But this provides only the weakest possible account of the owner’s special position: by default the owner is the only one at liberty to use the object after the exclusion of others.
While there is a grain of truth in the boundary theory inasmuch as ownership is an exclusive right, the boundary theory wrongly assumes that what it means for ownership to be exclusive is just that others generally have a duty to exclude themselves from the object owned. However, there is a distinction between a right’s being exclusive in the sense that it excludes others from the object of the right and its being exclusive in the sense that its holder occupies a special position that others do not share. A third theory, the “agenda-setting theory,” regards ownership as an exclusive right in the second sense but not the first. What it means for ownership to be exclusive is that owners are in a special position to set the agenda for a resource (e.g., farm owners determining the specific uses of their land). The law preserves the exclusivity of ownership not by excluding others, but by harmonizing their interests with the owner’s agenda-setting authority. This, rather than the boundary theory’s “exclusivity,” is the essence of ownership.
questions.stem: According to the author, the boundary theory’s method for distinguishing owners from nonowners

choices.A: exaggerates the rights and responsibilities of nonowners while unfairly placing the burden of proof of ownership on the owner
choices.B: entails that owners can be definitively distinguished from nonowners in every case
choices.C: leaves the rights and responsibilities unique to the position of ownership unexplained
choices.D: allows that some cases of judicial reasoning about ownership may be flawed
choices.E: uses one sense of “boundary” for owners and a different sense of “boundary” for nonowners

questions.explanation:
Process of elimination gives "only the weakest possible account of the owner's special position." The owner's unique position goes unexplained.
A — Burden of proof isn't mentioned.
B — Not claimed.
D — Flawed judicial reasoning isn't the issue.
E — No equivocation on "boundary."

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly implied by the bundle-of-rights theory expressed in the passage?

choices.A: Two owners of distinct properties might not possess the same rights regarding those properties.
choices.B: An owner is required to possess the material means of excluding others from the owned property.
choices.C: The agenda for an object owned must exclude nonowners from the use of the object.
choices.D: Ownership is an exclusive right because the concept of ownership is well defined.
choices.E: Ownership is an exclusive right because the concept of ownership is open ended.

questions.explanation:
Bundle theory: ownership is an open-ended set of rights arising from diverse decisions. Two owners might therefore hold different rights.
B — Material means of exclusion aren't part of any theory described.
C — Agenda-setting is a different theory, and it doesn't require excluding others.
D — Bundle theory says ownership is open-ended, not well defined.
E — Open-endedness is right, but bundle theory doesn't treat ownership as an exclusive right.

questions.stem: The author distinguishes two senses of “exclusive right” in the third paragraph primarily in order to

choices.A: offer an additional critique of the bundle-of-rights theory
choices.B: provide a way to distinguish the boundary theory from the agenda-setting theory
choices.C: suggest that the boundary theory is unintelligible despite having the appearance of truth
choices.D: explain the fundamental difference between the bundle-of-rights theory and the boundary theory
choices.E: show that all theories of ownership other than the agenda-setting theory are confused about the meaning of “exclusive”

questions.explanation:
Exclusivity as "excluding others" versus "a special position": the boundary theory uses the first, the agenda-setting theory the second.
A — Bundle theory isn't the target here.
C — The author grants the boundary theory a "grain of truth."
D — The distinction separates boundary from agenda-setting.
E — Only the boundary theory's view of exclusivity is criticized.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately defines “agenda” as it is used in the third paragraph?

choices.A: plan for use
choices.B: list of topics
choices.C: timetable of events
choices.D: task to be completed
choices.E: hidden motives

questions.explanation:
"Owners are in a special position to set the agenda for a resource (e.g., farm owners determining the specific uses of their land)." Agenda means plan for use.
B — The meeting sense of agenda.
C — Not about scheduling.
D — Not a single task.
E — The "hidden agenda" sense.

questions.stem: The author of the passage would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements regarding the boundary theory?

choices.A: It correctly identifies a key responsibility of owners but does not correctly analyze the nature of ownership itself.
choices.B: It was the chief target of criticism by the first legal scholars who promoted the bundle-of-rights theory.
choices.C: It correctly identifies a concept that is necessary for a valid theory of ownership but misinterprets that concept.
choices.D: It holds that ownership necessarily entails the right to sell the owned thing.
choices.E: It is derived from a more general theory of rights that is itself substantially correct.

questions.explanation:
"There is a grain of truth in the boundary theory inasmuch as ownership is an exclusive right," but it "wrongly assumes what it means" for ownership to be exclusive. Right concept, wrong interpretation.
A — The boundary theory focuses on nonowners' duty, not owners' responsibilities.
B — History of criticism isn't given.
D — The right to sell is part of the bundle examples, not the boundary theory.
E — No general theory of rights is mentioned.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 1 (Logical Reasoning), Q1
questions.stimulus: Critic: While the political message in this short story is interesting enough that the author could have based an essay, or a different short story, around that message alone, it should not have been included in this story. The story’s primary focus is humor, and the political message distracts from the story’s humorous effect.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most strongly supports the critic’s reasoning?
