choices.A: Authors should not convey political messages in their short stories.
choices.B: Nothing in a short story should distract from the story’s primary focus.
choices.C: Writers should not risk alienating readers who disagree with them politically.
choices.D: Political messages need to be developed differently in essays than in short stories.
choices.E: A short story’s political message is irrelevant to its artistic merit.

questions.explanation:
The story's primary focus is humor, and the political message distracts from it. So it shouldn't be there. The principle "nothing should distract from a story's primary focus" delivers that.
A — Bans political messages in all stories. The critic only objects because it distracts in this story.
C — Alienating readers isn't the critic's reason.
D — How messages develop in different forms isn't the reasoning.
E — Artistic merit isn't the critic's ground.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 1 (Logical Reasoning), Q2
questions.stimulus: Entertainment reporter: Unlike most major motion pictures, the release of the upcoming film Escapade II has not been preceded by free, advance screenings that show the film to select audiences for promotional purposes. With movie research showing awareness of the film at 96 percent, and with around 60 percent of filmgoers indicating “definite interest” in the film, the film’s distributors must have decided not to do anything that could reduce interest in the film.
questions.stem: The entertainment reporter’s explanation for why there have been no advance screenings of Escapade II relies on assuming that the distributors believe that

choices.A: advance screenings of Escapade II would cost them a significant amount that could much more effectively be spent on advertising
choices.B: advance screenings of Escapade II might lead to a dampening of the enthusiasm of filmgoers who would otherwise have an interest in seeing the film
choices.C: the select audiences who would normally be invited to free, advance screenings of a major motion picture would probably not enjoy Escapade II
choices.D: if 96 percent of the public is aware of the upcoming release of Escapade II, it is probable that 96 percent of the public intends to see the film
choices.E: the film Escapade II would most likely be viewed by approximately 60 percent of the public if no advance screenings are given

questions.explanation:
The reporter says distributors wanted to avoid anything that could reduce interest. Skipping screenings fits only if they think screenings might dampen enthusiasm.
A — Cost isn't in the reporter's explanation.
C — A specific version of the worry, but more than the explanation requires; it needs only that screenings might reduce interest.
D — Awareness doesn't become intent to see the film.
E — No such prediction is needed.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 1 (Logical Reasoning), Q3
questions.stimulus:
Anthropology professor: The new class I’m offering has been listed in the course catalog as a literature class, but it should be listed instead as an anthropology class. The texts we will study are all novels, but we will be examining them as sources of information about different cultures.
Dean: The class is listed as it should be. All the readings in the class are works of literature.
questions.stem: The dialogue provides the most support for the claim that the anthropology professor and the dean disagree over whether

choices.A: all of the books that will be read in the new class are novels
choices.B: a class can be listed as both an anthropology class and a literature class
choices.C: the approach taken to the readings should be a crucial determinant of how a class is listed
choices.D: the dean has the power to decide how a new class is to be listed
choices.E: an anthropology professor should be permitted to teach a literature class

questions.explanation:
The professor says the anthropological approach should determine the listing. The dean says the readings (literature) do. They disagree about whether the approach should be decisive.
A — Both accept the readings are novels/literature.
B — Neither raises double-listing.
D — Authority isn't discussed.
E — Who may teach what isn't at issue.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 1 (Logical Reasoning), Q4
questions.stimulus: Toy manufacturer: Our competitors argue that we should withdraw our KlopperKidz toys from stores because several children have allegedly been injured by them, and manufacturers should voluntarily withdraw toys that can lead to injury. Their allegations, however, have not been proved. Furthermore, even if they were proved, our competitors’ argument would still not merit serious attention, because their toys have caused injuries, and they have not volunteered to withdraw them from stores.
questions.stem: The toy manufacturer’s argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that it

choices.A: attempts to justify a conclusion by offering reasons that are mutually exclusive
choices.B: rejects an argument on the grounds that those making it have a vested interest in convincing people of the truth of the conclusion
choices.C: assumes that merely because something has not been proved to be true, it must therefore be false
choices.D: rejects an argument on the grounds that those making it have failed to abide by what the argument recommends
choices.E: takes a necessary condition for a toy’s being unsafe to be a sufficient condition for its being unsafe

questions.explanation:
The manufacturer dismisses the competitors' argument because the competitors don't withdraw their own injurious toys. Hypocrisy doesn't make an argument wrong.
A — "Not proved" and "even if proved" are compatible lines of reply.
B — The rejection rests on the competitors' failure to practice what they preach, not on their vested interest.
C — The manufacturer notes the claims are unproven but doesn't conclude they're false.
E — No necessary/sufficient confusion about safety.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 1 (Logical Reasoning), Q5
questions.stimulus: Researcher: Some scholars maintain that the first government other than China to issue any form of paper currency was the Massachusetts colony in 1690. But these scholars are incorrect. During a coin shortage in New France in 1685, its government was unable to use coins to pay soldiers stationed in Quebec. Instead, playing cards were assigned an official value and issued as pay. These cards, which could be used to buy goods, were convertible to coins, which later arrived on supply ships from France.
questions.stem: The researcher’s conclusion is properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: The playing cards in use in Quebec in the late 1600s were made of paper.
choices.B: The Chinese government did not issue paper currency during the 1600s.
choices.C: Playing cards were not available to inhabitants of the Massachusetts colony before 1690.
choices.D: The Massachusetts colony’s issue of paper currency was not prompted by a coin shortage.
choices.E: Every government that issued paper currency in the 1600s left records pertaining to that currency.

questions.explanation:
New France issued playing cards as currency in 1685, before Massachusetts in 1690. For that to count as the first paper currency, the cards must have been paper.
B — The claim is "other than China," so China's activity is irrelevant.
C — Massachusetts's access to cards doesn't matter.
D — Massachusetts's motive is irrelevant.
E — Record-keeping doesn't establish that the cards were paper.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 1 (Logical Reasoning), Q6
questions.stimulus: A tiny crab that lives 550 meters below the surface of the Gulf of Mexico has been found to have eyes that are sensitive to ultraviolet light. But ultraviolet light from the sun cannot penetrate to that depth. If the crab’s ultraviolet receptors developed as an adaptation to the depths, they are probably for detecting light from bioluminescent organisms. In that case, since the crab is not itself bioluminescent, it probably hunts bioluminescent prey.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument?

choices.A: A trait that serves no function tends to be lost over time.
choices.B: Prey is not plentiful at the depth at which the crabs are found.
choices.C: The crabs can detect each other by nonvisual means.
choices.D: It takes many generations to develop sensitivity to ultraviolet light.
choices.E: The crab’s most dangerous predators are bioluminescent.

questions.explanation:
The argument concludes the crab hunts bioluminescent prey. If its most dangerous predators are bioluminescent, the UV receptors could be for spotting predators instead.
A — Consistent with the receptors having some function. Doesn't pick between hunting and evading.
B — Scarce prey doesn't rule out hunting bioluminescent prey.
C — Detecting each other is irrelevant to UV vision's purpose.
D — Development time doesn't bear on function.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 1 (Logical Reasoning), Q7
questions.stimulus: Last year a local advertising agency produced many of its television commercials in a studio with improperly installed equipment. As a result, the sound in these commercials was not perfectly synchronized with the picture; this was particularly noticeable when people were shown talking, and it even prompted complaints from some viewers. However, local automobile dealerships that relied on television commercials from this agency tended to have greater sales increases during this period than did local dealerships using television commercials from other agencies instead.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the sales discrepancy described above?

choices.A: Most viewers turned off the sound on their televisions when local automobile-dealership commercials aired during this period.
choices.B: People are more likely to recall a television commercial they have seen if the sound and pictures were not properly synchronized.
choices.C: Most of the advertisers that relied on commercials produced at the studio with improperly installed equipment were automobile dealerships.
choices.D: Not all of the commercials produced for automobile dealerships at this studio contained video of people talking.
choices.E: Most of the local automobile dealerships during this time did not rely heavily on television advertising.

questions.explanation:
Badly synchronized ads were more memorable, so the flaw helped recall and sales.
A — Explains why poor sound didn't hurt, not why these dealerships did better.
C — Who used the studio doesn't explain the sales advantage.
D — Lessens the flaw's impact but doesn't explain the advantage.
E — Reliance on TV generally doesn't explain the difference.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 1 (Logical Reasoning), Q8
questions.stimulus: Sinking large, obsolete pieces of equipment in coral areas is said to provide much-needed habitats for marine life. This, proponents say, shows that the practice is ecologically sound. However, it may be that this practice is ecologically unsound even if it does provide much-needed habitats, for the practice may upset an area’s ecological balance in unknown ways.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the argument by the claim that the practice of sinking large, obsolete pieces of equipment in coral areas may upset an area’s ecological balance in unknown ways?

choices.A: It is intended to be a summary of the argument.
choices.B: It is a claim that the argument purports to refute.
choices.C: It is a claim that the argument contends is insufficient to show what some have taken it to show.
choices.D: It is the main conclusion of the argument.
choices.E: It is a premise of the argument.

questions.explanation:
The conclusion: the practice may be unsound even if it provides habitat. The reason ("for") is that it may upset ecological balance. It's a premise.
A — It isn't a summary.
B — The argument asserts it.
C — That describes the habitat claim, which the argument says doesn't show the practice is sound.
D — The conclusion is the "may be ecologically unsound" claim.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 1 (Logical Reasoning), Q9
questions.stimulus: Having cameras at traffic intersections to automatically ticket cars that run red lights might raise revenue for municipalities but does not increase traffic safety. Accidents actually increase at intersections that have cameras: There are fewer side-impact collisions but significantly more rear-impact collisions.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.A: The revenue raised through automatically generated tickets can be used to address issues other than traffic safety.
choices.B: Automatically generated tickets for running red lights have been shown to generate some undeserved tickets.
choices.C: Side-impact collisions are generally the fault of the driver who drives through the red light.
choices.D: Side-impact collisions are a much greater safety threat than rear-impact collisions.
choices.E: Automatically generated tickets can punish the owner of the car rather than the driver of the car at the time of the infraction.

questions.explanation:
The argument counts accidents. If the side-impact collisions cameras prevent are far more dangerous than the extra rear-end ones, safety may improve.
A — Revenue use is irrelevant to safety.
B — Undeserved tickets don't bear on safety.
C — Fault isn't safety.
E — Who gets punished is irrelevant.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 1 (Logical Reasoning), Q10
questions.stimulus: For years, Glenville had the highest apartment rents in the metropolitan region in which it is located. This year, Glenville has only the third highest apartment rents in the region. Therefore, it must cost less to rent an apartment in Glenville now than it used to.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments demonstrates most effectively by parallel reasoning that the argument above is flawed?

choices.A: Because Brenda’s kitten’s veterinary bills are lower than her puppy’s veterinary bills, the kitten must be healthier than the puppy.
choices.B: Because Brenda’s kitten was larger than her puppy a while ago but is now smaller than the puppy, the kitten must have shrunk.
choices.C: Because Brenda’s kitten was born a week before her puppy was, Brenda must have gotten the kitten first.
choices.D: Because Brenda’s kitten eats less than her puppy does, the kitten is unlikely to become overweight.
choices.E: Because Brenda’s kitten has become more friendly toward her puppy recently, the puppy must have become more friendly toward the kitten.

questions.explanation:
Glenville's rank dropped, but its rents could have stayed put or risen while others rose faster. The kitten "must have shrunk" makes the same leap from a relative change to an absolute one.
A — Different flaw (cost to health).
C — Birth order versus acquisition. A different flaw.
D — A prediction from intake, not a ranking change.
E — Reciprocity assumption. A different flaw.

traps.A: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure
traps.C: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure
traps.D: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure
traps.E: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 1 (Logical Reasoning), Q11
questions.stimulus: The crocodiles of Lake Victoria, in East Africa, sometimes attack humans that venture into their habitat. The number of attacks on people by these crocodiles has increased significantly in the last 20 years. This is despite the fact that the number of crocodiles in the lake has not increased in that time and the crocodiles have no less food available.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the increase in the incidence of crocodile attacks on humans?

choices.A: Wildlife authorities on Lake Victoria sometimes destroy crocodiles that they believe to be responsible for attacks on humans.
choices.B: About 100 crocodiles inhabit the part of Lake Victoria where most of the attacks on humans have occurred.
choices.C: More attacks on humans by crocodiles occur in Lake Victoria than in any other part of Africa.
choices.D: Adult crocodiles in Lake Victoria are generally unafraid of humans or their boats.
choices.E: People now fish in more parts of Lake Victoria than they did in previous decades.

questions.explanation:
Same number of crocodiles and enough food, but more attacks. If people now fish in more of the lake, they enter crocodile habitat more often.
A — Killing problem crocodiles would reduce attacks.
B — A population figure doesn't explain an increase.
C — A comparison with other places doesn't explain change over time.
D — A constant trait doesn't explain an increase.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 1 (Logical Reasoning), Q12
questions.stimulus: When the annual period of daylight saving time begins, and clocks are set forward one hour, many people lose an hour of sleep. On the following day, according to government statistics, the incidence of traffic accidents is 7 percent greater than the average for that time of year. It is therefore likely that sleep deprivation is responsible for this spike in traffic accidents.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.A: Many people forget to set their clocks forward when daylight saving time begins and are late for appointments on the following day as a result.
choices.B: Traffic accidents are less common in the spring, when the annual period of daylight saving time begins, than they are in the winter.
choices.C: The traffic accidents that occur on the day after daylight saving time begins are no more severe than normal.
choices.D: The higher incidence of accidents is most pronounced later in the day, when sleep-deprived people tend to be most drowsy.
choices.E: The effects of sleep deprivation can linger for several days.

questions.explanation:
If accidents peak when sleep-deprived people are drowsiest, that ties the spike to sleep loss.
A — Forgetting to change clocks and rushing is an alternative cause.
B — The comparison is already to the average for that time of year.
C — Severity doesn't bear on the cause.
E — Lingering effects might predict elevated accidents on later days, which isn't reported. Neutral at best.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 1 (Logical Reasoning), Q13
questions.stimulus: Every human’s brain contains a mental representation of the external world. Yet, this representation necessarily leaves out much detail. After all, the external world is much larger and more complex than the human brain, and there is no way an object could completely represent something larger and more complex than itself.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the conclusion drawn in the argument?

choices.A: The human brain’s representation of the external world leaves out much detail.
choices.B: The external world is much larger and more complex than a human brain.
choices.C: The human brain cannot completely represent something larger and more complex than itself.
choices.D: The human brain contains a mental representation of the external world.
choices.E: It is impossible for any entity to completely represent anything larger and more complicated than itself.

questions.explanation:
"Yet this representation necessarily leaves out much detail. After all..." The "after all" clauses support that claim.
B — A premise.
C — Follows from the general principle, as support.
D — Background.
E — The general principle used as a premise.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 1 (Logical Reasoning), Q14
questions.stimulus: Generally, open discussion of a false and pernicious idea diminishes its appeal. Even in a flourishing democracy, however, certain misconceptions are so alluring that they tend to gain in popularity when they are debated.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles is most clearly illustrated by the statements above?

choices.A: Democratic governments should be allowed on occasion to suppress debate regarding certain misconceptions.
choices.B: Sometimes it is better to openly discuss an idea even though doing so will increase the popularity of a misconception.
choices.C: Not all pernicious ideas are misconceptions.
choices.D: Discussion and debate do not necessarily lead to a greater acceptance of the truth.
choices.E: One of the reasons some ideas are appealing is that they are false.

questions.explanation:
Usually discussion weakens bad ideas, but some misconceptions gain popularity when debated. So discussion doesn't necessarily lead toward the truth.
A — Suppression isn't endorsed.
B — No judgment about when discussion is better.
C — The stimulus treats these misconceptions as pernicious ideas. It doesn't separate the two.
E — Falsity as a source of appeal isn't stated.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 1 (Logical Reasoning), Q15
questions.stimulus:
Schmidt: In enforcing township rules on how homeowners maintain their property, it is a mistake to encourage residents to report violations by their neighbors. Doing so engenders bad feelings among neighbors and leads to tips based on spite.
Chandha: It’s not a mistake. Without rules on how homeowners maintain their property, a single homeowner could degrade the appearance of an entire neighborhood.
questions.stem: Chandha’s response is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: takes a criticism of the way in which certain rules are enforced to be a criticism of the rules themselves
choices.B: challenges the motivation behind Schmidt’s argument rather than Schmidt’s reasoning
choices.C: confuses a criticism of the consequences of having a set of rules with a criticism of the detailed provisions of the rules
choices.D: takes for granted that just because something is likely to happen on some occasions, it will always happen
choices.E: confuses the cause of bad feelings among neighbors with a consequence of bad feelings among neighbors

questions.explanation:
Schmidt criticizes encouraging neighbors to report violations, a method of enforcement. Chandha defends having rules at all.
B — Chandha doesn't discuss Schmidt's motives.
C — Schmidt criticizes enforcement, not consequences of the rules or their provisions.
D — No overgeneralization.
E — No causal confusion.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 1 (Logical Reasoning), Q16
questions.stimulus: Some have argued that once it becomes necessary for us to think about computers in terms of beliefs and desires in order to understand how they function, we can rightly say that computers have beliefs and desires. However, we already need to think about what computers believe and desire in order to understand how they function, and thus the suggested criterion for ascribing beliefs and desires to computers implies that the computers that exist now have beliefs and desires. So the suggested criterion is obviously flawed.
questions.stem: The claim that the computers that exist now have beliefs and desires plays which one of the following roles in the argument above?

choices.A: It is held to be an unacceptable conclusion to which the suggested criterion would lead.
choices.B: It is a view the argument assumes is uncontroversial.
choices.C: It is an example given to clarify the criterion in question.
choices.D: It is the conclusion of the argument.
choices.E: It is a premise whose truth is necessary to the success of the argument.

questions.explanation:
The criterion implies today's computers have beliefs and desires, which the author treats as absurd. So the criterion is flawed. It's the unacceptable consequence.
B — The argument treats it as false.
C — Not offered as clarification.
D — The conclusion is that the criterion is flawed.
E — The argument needs it to be false, not true.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 1 (Logical Reasoning), Q17
questions.stimulus: Manufacturer: If our biggest competitor were to go out of business, some of the specialized suppliers that we both use would be bankrupted. So, in order for us to stay in business, our biggest competitor must stay in business.
questions.stem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: The manufacturer’s specialized suppliers will not be bankrupted.
choices.B: The manufacturer will stay in business if its biggest competitor stays in business.
choices.C: If the manufacturer goes out of business, its biggest competitor will go out of business.
choices.D: The manufacturer will stay in business if its specialized suppliers are not bankrupted.
choices.E: The manufacturer will stay in business only if its specialized suppliers are not bankrupted.

questions.explanation:
Premise: competitor out → suppliers bankrupt. Needed: manufacturer stays → suppliers not bankrupt. Then manufacturer stays → suppliers OK → competitor stays (contrapositive of the premise).
A — Asserting suppliers survive doesn't give the conditional.
B — Gives competitor stays → manufacturer stays, the reverse of the conclusion.
C — Gives manufacturer out → competitor out, not what's needed.
D — Makes surviving suppliers sufficient, not necessary.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 1 (Logical Reasoning), Q18
questions.stimulus: Jack’s dog howls whenever a train goes by. Occasionally a train goes by while Jack is washing his dog. So Jack’s dog must sometimes howl while he is washing it.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following arguments is most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.A: Every serious jogger can benefit from good running shoes. But there must be a few serious joggers who prefer to run in ordinary sneakers, since some people who can benefit from good running shoes prefer to run in ordinary sneakers.
choices.B: Most serious joggers can benefit from good running shoes. But some serious joggers prefer to run in ordinary sneakers. So some people who prefer to run in ordinary sneakers can benefit from good running shoes.
choices.C: Any serious jogger can benefit from good running shoes. But a few serious joggers prefer to run in ordinary sneakers. So some people who can benefit from good running shoes prefer to run in ordinary sneakers.
choices.D: At least some serious joggers can benefit from good running shoes. But there are serious joggers who prefer to run in ordinary sneakers. So some people who prefer to run in ordinary sneakers can benefit from good running shoes.
choices.E: Any serious jogger can benefit from good running shoes. But some serious joggers occasionally prefer to run in ordinary sneakers. So anyone who can benefit from good running shoes occasionally prefers to run in ordinary sneakers.

questions.explanation:
Original: all A are B (train → howl); some A are C (some trains pass during washing); so some C are B. Joggers: all serious joggers benefit; some serious joggers prefer sneakers; so some who benefit prefer sneakers.
A — Draws a conclusion about serious joggers from the reverse direction. Invalid.
B — "Most" in the first premise breaks the guarantee.
D — "Some" in the first premise breaks the guarantee.
E — Concludes "anyone," which overgeneralizes.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 1 (Logical Reasoning), Q19
questions.stimulus: When plants are growing quickly, they take more carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere than they release into it. But when they are growing very slowly, the reverse is true. Any substantial increase in the amount of carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere causes temperatures to increase in the tropics, where the bulk of Earth’s plants are found. And the more temperatures increase in the tropics, the more slowly, on average, the plants there grow.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: The amount of carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere will inevitably increase at a gradually accelerating rate of speed.
choices.B: If the amount of carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere increases substantially, the bulk of Earth’s plants will release more carbon dioxide into the atmosphere than they take out of it.
choices.C: Plants in the tropics will grow more slowly, on average, if they release enough carbon dioxide to increase substantially the total amount of carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere.
choices.D: If the plants in the tropics begin to grow more slowly, on average, the temperatures in the tropics will increase substantially as a result.
choices.E: Any increase in temperatures in the tropics will be associated with a substantial increase in the amount of carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere.

questions.explanation:
Substantially more CO2 released → tropical temperatures rise → tropical plants grow more slowly. If the plants themselves cause that substantial release, the chain still applies.
A — Nothing says it will inevitably accelerate.
B — Plants grow more slowly, but "very slowly" (when they release more than they absorb) isn't guaranteed.
D — Reverses the temperature–growth link.
E — Reverses the CO2–temperature link.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 1 (Logical Reasoning), Q20
questions.stimulus: Essayist: Since ancient times humans have relied on myths to try to explain our place in the cosmos. In this respect the claims of science are not different from stories about the gods of Homer. The question of the truth of science, as with myth, is merely the question of how well it helps us to cope with the human condition. So while science undoubtedly can count some successes, that it falls short of complete truth is amply demonstrated by the degree to which science is responsible for the breakdown of society’s key institutions.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main conclusion of the essayist’s argument?

choices.A: Science is at least in part responsible for the breakdown of key institutions in society.
choices.B: Science is no more true than the myth of the gods of Homer.
choices.C: Science is only partially true.
choices.D: Science is merely a myth.
choices.E: Science, like stories about the gods of Homer, attempts to explain our place in the cosmos.

questions.explanation:
"That it falls short of complete truth is amply demonstrated." Science is only partially true.
A — Used as evidence.
B — A comparison implied by the setup, but not the conclusion. The essayist grants science some successes.
D — Not claimed.
E — A premise.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 1 (Logical Reasoning), Q21
questions.stimulus: Sodium nitrate is frequently added to sausages to make them pink. However, sodium nitrate does not contribute to preventing spoilage of the meat, and excessive use of it increases the level of sodium in the sausages beyond what is necessary for good taste. Because consumption of an excessive level of sodium can lead to health problems, clearly sodium nitrate should never be added to sausages.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on which one of the following grounds?

choices.A: The argument makes a recommendation based on evidence from an insufficient sample.
choices.B: The argument does not address possible risks associated with the proposed recommendation.
choices.C: The argument presumes, without providing justification, that it is appropriate for the government to protect people from possible health threats without their consent.
choices.D: The argument does not provide sufficient justification for preferring the solution it recommends over more moderate alternatives.
choices.E: The argument does not distinguish adequately between medical and economic justifications for a policy.

questions.explanation:
The evidence concerns excessive use, but the conclusion is "never" add it. Moderate amounts aren't shown to be harmful.
A — No sample is involved.
B — Risks of not adding it aren't the main flaw.
C — No government role is claimed.
E — No economic justification appears.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 1 (Logical Reasoning), Q22
questions.stimulus: For a zoo to make a valuable contribution to the community, it must be well run. All large zoos that are well run have some full-time veterinarians on staff, but many small zoos that are well run have only part-time veterinarians. In addition, there are many large zoos that make valuable contributions to their communities and are open all year, while most small zoos are closed in winter.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, then which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: Most large zoos are well run.
choices.B: No large, well-run zoos have any part-time veterinarians on staff.
choices.C: Some zoos that make valuable contributions to their communities have only part-time veterinarians on staff.
choices.D: Some zoos that are open all year have full-time veterinarians on staff.
choices.E: Most small zoos make valuable contributions to their communities.

questions.explanation:
Many large zoos make valuable contributions and are open all year. Valuable contribution → well run, and large well-run zoos have full-time vets. So those zoos, which are open all year, have full-time vets.
A — "Many" doesn't mean most.
B — Full-time vets don't exclude part-time ones too.
C — Small well-run zoos might not make valuable contributions.
E — Unsupported.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 1 (Logical Reasoning), Q23
questions.stimulus: Principal: All of our school’s rural students participate in the school’s lunch program because they live too far away to go home for lunch, while roughly one half of their urban counterparts also take part in the program. Some participants in this program, including some of the school’s strongest academic achievers, also participate in extracurricular activities such as sports and drama. Therefore, we know that some of the participants in extracurricular activities are rural students and some are urban students.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the principal’s argument is flawed because this argument

choices.A: takes for granted that a greater number of strong academic achievers than those who are not strong academic achievers participate in extracurricular activities
choices.B: takes for granted that a greater number of rural students than urban students participate in extracurricular activities
choices.C: ignores the possibility that those who participate both in the lunch program and in extracurricular activities do not include both urban and rural students
choices.D: ignores the possibility that both rural and urban students have many other ways of occupying their time besides extracurricular activities
choices.E: at first uses the word “participate” in one sense and then illicitly allows the word’s meaning to change

questions.explanation:
Some lunch participants do extracurriculars, but those could all be rural, or all urban. Nothing ensures both groups are represented.
A — Strong achievers are incidental.
B — No numbers are compared.
D — Other activities don't bear on the inference.
E — "Participate" keeps the same meaning.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 1 (Logical Reasoning), Q24
questions.stimulus:
Principle: An author of an article that has appeared in a magazine should be allowed to respond in that magazine to harsh criticism of the article if the criticism was published in the same magazine, or, alternatively, if the criticism was published in another magazine and is unfair.
Application: McFinton should be allowed to publish a response in Speculator’s Digest to Wallace’s most recent article, because Wallace’s article is harshly critical of McFinton’s essay on self-deception.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, justifies the above application of the principle?

choices.A: McFinton’s essay on self-deception appeared in Speculator’s Digest as well as in other magazines.
choices.B: Wallace’s most recent article was published in Speculator’s Digest as well as in other magazines.
choices.C: McFinton’s essay on self-deception appeared only in Speculator’s Digest, while Wallace’s article has been published in a wide array of other magazines.
choices.D: Both McFinton’s essay on self-deception and Wallace’s most recent article were published in Speculator’s Digest.
choices.E: Wallace’s most recent article appeared in Speculator’s Digest and was unfair in its harsh criticism of McFinton’s essay on self-deception.

questions.explanation:
The principle's first clause: the author's article and the harsh criticism both appeared in the same magazine. Both McFinton's essay and Wallace's article in Speculator's Digest satisfy it.
A — Doesn't establish Wallace's criticism appeared there.
B — Doesn't establish McFinton's essay appeared there.
C — Wallace's article appeared elsewhere, so the second clause would need unfairness, which isn't given.
E — Doesn't establish McFinton's essay appeared in Speculator's Digest, where he'd respond.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 1 (Logical Reasoning), Q25
questions.stimulus: Paleontologist: Most biologists accept that birds evolved from dinosaurs known as maniraptors. Some biologists have not accepted this theory, because the oldest known bird fossils predate the oldest known maniraptor fossils by several million years. This reasoning is misguided, however; the fact that no maniraptor fossils of a certain age have been discovered hardly rules out the possibility that such fossils exist.
questions.stem: The paleontologist’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on which one of the following grounds?

choices.A: It overlooks the possibility that even if a particular argument against a theory is misguided, that theory may nonetheless be untrue.
choices.B: It fails to address adequately the possibility that even if maniraptors existed before the first birds did, there may not be any maniraptor fossils older than the oldest known bird fossils.
choices.C: It takes for granted that if there are any maniraptor fossils older than the oldest known bird fossils, this itself proves that birds evolved from maniraptors.
choices.D: It overlooks the possibility that there may be substantial evidence that birds did not evolve from maniraptors, but that this evidence may be unrelated to the ages of any known or unknown bird and maniraptor fossils.
choices.E: It fails to address adequately the possibility that it can be reasonable to refuse to accept a theory solely on the grounds that the evidence yet discovered for the theory appears to be insufficient.

questions.explanation:
The skeptics withhold acceptance because current evidence looks insufficient. The paleontologist calls this misguided merely because older fossils might exist. Withholding acceptance until evidence appears can be reasonable.
A — The paleontologist doesn't conclude the theory is true, only that one objection is misguided.
B — Doesn't identify a flaw in calling the skeptics misguided.
C — The paleontologist claims no such proof.
D — Other evidence is beside the point of this narrow argument.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q1
questions.stimulus:
Parikh: Jon has at least three unpaid parking tickets, so it’s clear that he has no respect for the law.
Atler: Although Jon does have too many unpaid parking tickets, these few minor infractions indicate nothing more than that he might be lazy or careless.
questions.stem: The dialogue provides the most support for the claim that Parikh and Atler disagree over whether there is evidence that Jon

choices.A: has at least three unpaid parking tickets
choices.B: has no respect for the law
choices.C: has committed a few minor infractions
choices.D: has too many unpaid parking tickets
choices.E: might be lazy or careless

questions.explanation:
Parikh says the tickets show Jon has no respect for the law. Atler says they show nothing more than possible laziness or carelessness.
A — Atler concedes Jon has the tickets.
C — Atler calls them minor infractions; Parikh doesn't dispute that they're infractions.
D — Atler agrees he has too many.
E — Only Atler raises laziness, and Parikh never denies it.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q2
questions.stimulus: The nests inhabited by wood rats often contain nibbled bay and oak leaves. Since only the oak leaves are a known food source, the bay leaves are probably placed there to act as a fumigant to reduce parasites such as fleas. This view is backed by an experiment in which some flea larvae were incubated with torn bay leaves and some with torn oak leaves. The survival rate with oak leaves was close to 100 percent, but with bay leaves just one in four larvae survived.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.A: Wood rats that live near oak trees almost invariably have oak leaves in their nests.
choices.B: Wood rats are the only rodents that have been found to keep nibbled bay leaves in their nests.
choices.C: Most wood rat nests that do not contain nibbled bay leaves are infested with fleas.
choices.D: Fleas more commonly live on wood rats themselves than in the nests of wood rats.
choices.E: Bay leaves are generally more difficult for wood rats to gather than oak leaves are.

questions.explanation:
The claim: bay leaves fumigate nests against fleas. If nests without bay leaves are mostly flea-infested, that fits the protective role.
A — Oak leaves near oak trees doesn't speak to the bay leaves' purpose.
B — Uniqueness among rodents doesn't support the fumigant function.
D — If fleas mostly live on the rats, a nest fumigant matters less.
E — Extra effort hints at purpose but doesn't identify that purpose as fumigation.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q3
questions.stimulus: Of all the commonly consumed foods, eggs contain the highest amount of dietary cholesterol, which contributes to people’s blood cholesterol levels. Yet when people who stop eating eggs for breakfast are monitored over the course of a year, their blood cholesterol levels are often found to increase.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.A: Although eggs are high in dietary cholesterol, they also contain substances such as protein and vitamins, which are beneficial to overall health.
choices.B: Among people with certain health conditions, there is a high correlation between egg consumption and elevated blood cholesterol.
choices.C: People who stop eating eggs for breakfast generally do so because of concern about their cholesterol levels.
choices.D: Many people who regularly eat eggs for breakfast have about the same level of cholesterol in their blood as people who have never eaten eggs for breakfast.
choices.E: Many people who stop eating eggs for breakfast start eating breakfast foods that are high in saturated fat, which has a greater effect on blood cholesterol than dietary cholesterol does.

questions.explanation:
Quitters often switch to saturated-fat breakfasts, which raise blood cholesterol more than eggs do. So levels can rise after dropping eggs.
A — Other nutrients don't explain rising cholesterol.
B — A correlation in some groups doesn't explain the increase.
C — Explains why people quit, not why levels rise.
D — Similar levels among egg eaters don't explain an increase after quitting.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q4
questions.stimulus: An enormous, recently completed resort is the largest project ever built to environmental building standards. However, the resort is an economic failure—most of its many hotel rooms are empty—and it is thus no great achievement in environmental sustainability either.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning in the argument?

choices.A: Environmental sustainability is no less difficult to achieve with resort facilities than with other kinds of facilities.
choices.B: Using resources to build things that the market does not demand compromises environmental sustainability.
choices.C: Buildings designed for recreational uses should be built to the same standards as buildings designed for industrial uses.
choices.D: To minimize risk, large construction projects should not be undertaken during a time of economic instability.
choices.E: Reducing energy used during operation of a building is more important than reducing energy used to construct the building.

questions.explanation:
From economic failure (empty rooms) to "no great sustainability achievement." The principle that building what the market doesn't demand compromises sustainability bridges that.
A — Difficulty compared across facility types isn't the reasoning.
C — Building standards across uses aren't at issue.
D — Timing and economic instability aren't the reasoning.
E — Operation versus construction energy isn't the reasoning.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q5
questions.stimulus: IlluminCo should focus its efforts on developing affordable light-emitting diode (LED) bulbs for widespread use. LED bulbs have many advantages over incandescent and fluorescent bulbs. Because their design is simpler, LED bulbs undergo less wear and tear than other bulbs and consequently last much longer. In addition, LED bulbs use significantly less energy than do other bulbs. However, because of their cost, LED bulbs are currently used only in limited applications.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion drawn in the argument?

choices.A: IlluminCo should focus on developing affordable LED bulbs for widespread use.
choices.B: LED bulbs have many advantages over incandescent and fluorescent bulbs.
choices.C: LED bulbs last much longer than incandescent and fluorescent bulbs.
choices.D: LED bulbs use significantly less energy than do other bulbs.
choices.E: Because of their cost, LED bulbs are currently used only in limited applications.

questions.explanation:
The first sentence is the recommendation; the rest give reasons and context.
B — A supporting premise.
C — A supporting detail.
D — A supporting detail.
E — Context explaining why "affordable" matters.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q6
questions.stimulus:
Nguyen: The recently discovered structure at Aila, which dates from about 300 A.D., has been labeled “the oldest Christian church.” But it is not the oldest, for the Christian church at Doura-Europos, a city destroyed in 250 A.D., is at least half a century older.
Parker: Well, the earliest Christians worshiped in private houses, not churches as such, and the Doura-Europos structure was a private house converted into a structure for Christian worship, whereas the Aila structure was built expressly as a Christian church.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the grounds on which Parker criticizes Nguyen’s reasoning?

choices.A: The term “church” can refer to an organization rather than a structure.
choices.B: The term “church” cannot be appropriately applied to the structure at Doura-Europos.
choices.C: Nguyen uses the term “church” to mean two different things.
choices.D: There is insufficient evidence for the existence of the structure at Aila.
choices.E: There is no evidence that the earliest Christians worshiped in structures built expressly as churches.

questions.explanation:
Parker says Doura-Europos was a converted private house, not a church as such, while Aila was built as a church. So "church" doesn't properly apply to Doura-Europos.
A — Parker discusses structures, not organizations.
C — Parker's objection is that Nguyen misapplies the term to Doura-Europos, not that Nguyen equivocates within his argument.
D — Aila's existence isn't questioned.
E — Parker says the earliest Christians used private houses but doesn't make this evidence claim.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q7
questions.stimulus: Judith usually eats in Thai restaurants, because Thai food is her favorite kind. Thus, since Pablo usually eats in Italian restaurants, evidently Italian food is his favorite kind.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.A: takes what is evidently a difference of degree to be a difference of kind
choices.B: infers from the effect an action has that the action is intended to have that effect
choices.C: infers that simply because a set of things taken as a whole has a certain property, each member of that set has the property
choices.D: confuses an absence of evidence against a claim with the existence of evidence in support of that claim
choices.E: proceeds as if a given kind of causal explanation can be generalized on the basis of a single instance

questions.explanation:
Judith's habit is explained by her preference. The argument assumes the same explanation fits Pablo. He might eat Italian for price or location.
A — No degree versus kind confusion.
B — No inference about intent.
C — No whole-to-part move.
D — No absence-of-evidence move.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q8
questions.stimulus: Plaintiff’s lawyer: The judge in this case recently went on a skiing weekend with a small group that included the defendant. Moreover, before the case arose, the judge’s family occasionally received complimentary tickets to theater and sporting events from the defendant’s company. So, even if the judge’s avowal that the case was never discussed during the skiing weekend is accurate, her connections with the defendant raise doubts about whether she can decide it impartially. She should do the right thing and step down from the case.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning in the plaintiff’s lawyer’s argument?

choices.A: Because they are human, judges should not ever be expected to be completely impartial in deciding a case.
choices.B: Judges should always disqualify themselves from cases in which any reasonable question can be raised about their impartiality.
choices.C: A judge’s claim that she has not discussed a case with one of the parties to it should be viewed with suspicion if the judge has received something of value from that party.
choices.D: A judge should step down from a case if there is clear evidence that the judge has been unfairly influenced by one of the parties to it.
choices.E: A judge should never accept items of value from someone who is a defendant in a case over which she is presiding.

questions.explanation:
Even granting the judge didn't discuss the case, her connections raise doubts about impartiality. The principle "step down whenever a reasonable question about impartiality arises" delivers the conclusion.
A — Expecting imperfection doesn't call for recusal.
C — About doubting her claim. The lawyer's reasoning holds "even if" the claim is accurate.
D — Requires clear evidence of influence, which the lawyer doesn't claim.
E — The gifts came before the case. And it says nothing about stepping down.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q9
questions.stimulus: A recent experiment shows that chimpanzees sometimes act not out of self-interest, but altruistically. In this experiment, chimpanzees watched a person unknown to them reach through the bars of their enclosure for a stick. When the person was unable to reach it, most of the chimpanzees handed the stick to the person even though they had to make an effort to reach it. Since no reward was offered to the chimpanzees in the experiment, what it revealed was clearly altruism.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.A: The chimpanzees in the experiment did not have an expectation that they would be rewarded.
choices.B: If a reward had been offered in the experiment, the chimpanzees would have behaved differently.
choices.C: Chimpanzees are the only nonhumans that have been shown to exhibit altruistic behavior.
choices.D: The chimpanzees in the experiment considered retrieving the stick to be a form of play.
choices.E: The chimpanzees would have behaved differently had they been familiar with the person who reached through the bars of their enclosure.

questions.explanation:
"No reward was offered" proves altruism only if the chimps didn't expect one anyway. If they expected payment, self-interest remains possible.
B — Not required. Altruism doesn't depend on how they'd act with a reward.
C — Uniqueness is irrelevant.
D — Play would suggest self-interest, which undercuts altruism.
E — Familiarity isn't required.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q10
questions.stimulus:
Dr.
Cortez: Dr. Brady claims her research shows that the best choice for people at risk for a heart attack is to avoid exercising outdoors on days when there are high levels of air pollution. This conclusion is obviously wrong. It would be far better to remove pollution from the air than to just avoid it.
questions.stem: Dr. Cortez’s reasoning is questionable in that it

choices.A: criticizes an argument by attacking the person making the argument rather than the content of the argument being made
choices.B: mistakes what is meant to be advice directed at individuals for a recommendation about public policy
choices.C: infers that something is best for a group as a whole simply on the grounds that it is best for individual members of that group
choices.D: presumes, without providing justification, that only those at risk for a heart attack should avoid exercising outdoors on days when there are high levels of air pollution
choices.E: takes for granted that the removal of pollution from the air would be a good thing when that is one of the issues in dispute

questions.explanation:
Brady advises at-risk individuals what to do on polluted days. Cortez answers with a policy goal (remove pollution), which isn't an option for an individual.
A — Cortez addresses the claim, not Brady personally.
C — No part-to-whole move.
D — Cortez doesn't presume that.
E — Whether removing pollution is good isn't the issue in dispute.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q11
questions.stimulus: When campaigning for office, politicians sometimes promise to do things that they believe would be contrary to the interests of the public. Once in office, however, a politician who gets elected should try to keep any campaign promises that the politician believes would not make the public worse off.
questions.stem: The principle stated above, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning in which one of the following arguments?

choices.A: Greeley was elected to office on the promise to reduce taxes. Upon taking office it became apparent to Greeley that reducing taxes would require cuts in services that would be unpopular with the public. Thus, Greeley should not try to reduce taxes.
choices.B: Zamora believes that building the water treatment plant will not make the public better off, but that promising to do so will help Zamora get elected, and that electing Zamora will be in the public’s best interest. Thus, it is not wrong for Zamora to make the promise.
choices.C: Najera campaigned on a promise to preserve funding for a new recycling center. Once in office, Najera came to doubt that fulfilling the promise would provide any benefit to the public. Thus, Najera should break the promise.
choices.D: Yan campaigned on the promise to increase spending on road maintenance despite believing that fulfilling the promise would be to the detriment of the public. But once elected, Yan concluded that fulfilling the promise would benefit the public. So Yan should keep the promise.
choices.E: Kourik campaigned on the promise to restructure the Housing Department. Once in office, Kourik concluded that attempting to restructure the Housing Department would be to the public’s detriment. Thus, Kourik never should have promised to restructure the Housing Department.

questions.explanation:
Keep any promise you believe won't make the public worse off. Yan now believes the promise benefits the public, so he should keep it.
A — Unpopular cuts aren't shown to make the public worse off, and the principle says to keep such promises.
B — About making promises, not keeping them.
C — Doubting a benefit isn't believing harm. The principle says keep it.
E — About whether the promise should have been made.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q12
questions.stimulus: Suvaine is a drug that is prescribed to alleviate symptoms associated with a skin disorder. When it became known that the incidence of certain cancers is higher among people taking Suvaine than it is for people of the same age in the general population, some physicians hypothesized that taking Suvaine contributes to cancer risk.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to assess the support for the physicians’ hypothesis?

choices.A: whether the incidence of the cancers is the same among people with the skin disorder as it is for people who do not have the skin disorder
choices.B: whether any other drugs alleviate the symptoms of the skin disorder as well as Suvaine does
choices.C: whether the number of people taking Suvaine increased significantly just before the discovery about the incidence of the cancers
choices.D: whether there has recently been an increase in the overall incidence of the types of cancer found to have a relatively high incidence among people taking Suvaine
choices.E: whether people ever use Suvaine for any purpose other than alleviating symptoms associated with the skin disorder

questions.explanation:
People taking Suvaine have the skin disorder. If the disorder itself goes with these cancers, the drug may be blameless.
B — Alternative drugs don't test causation.
C — Usage trends don't test the link.
D — Overall trends affect everyone, but the comparison is with same-age peers.
E — Other uses matter little; the key confounder is the disorder.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q13
questions.stimulus: Many toll roads have added methods of collecting tolls by automatically debiting the prepaid accounts of drivers whose vehicles pass by an electronic sensor rather than by making drivers stop to pay. Promoters claim that the savings involved allows tolls to remain lower than they otherwise would be. However, a recent study shows that when electronic payment systems are in place toll increases are 30 percent higher than they are on roads without electronic payment systems.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.A: Electronic payment systems have environmental advantages because they reduce the traffic delays associated with traditional toll collection.
choices.B: Not all drivers who use toll roads use them enough to make it worth their while to set up an account and acquire the equipment needed to use an electronic system.
choices.C: When drivers do not take time to pay the cost of each trip on a toll road separately, they are less likely to put pressure on the road’s managers to keep toll charges down.
choices.D: By taking payment in advance of actual trips, electronic payment systems have a financial advantage through the accrual of interest.
choices.E: Toll increases are an effective strategy for encouraging drivers to carpool, thereby reducing congestion.

questions.explanation:
Drivers who don't pay per trip feel the charges less and push back less, so managers raise tolls more.
A — Environmental benefits don't explain higher increases.
B — Adoption rates don't explain toll levels.
D — A financial advantage would support lower tolls.
E — A reason to raise tolls in general, not tied to electronic systems.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q14
questions.stimulus: By inserting genes from a certain common vegetable into the vines of wine grapes, researchers have created grapevines that survive very cold winters. This research is useless, however. Even if good wines can be made from these grapes, consumers will not accept wine made from grapes with vegetable genes.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.A: Techniques developed in the course of the research could also be used to make wine grapes more cold tolerant by inserting genes from cold-tolerant wild grapes.
choices.B: Grapes from the vines that the researchers developed have not been tested to determine their suitability for wine making.
choices.C: Every year, grapevines at many vineyards are destroyed by cold weather.
choices.D: If winemakers ever make wine from grapes with genetic material from another type of fruit or vegetable, they will be obligated to disclose that information on their labels.
choices.E: Some very good wines are made from grapes grown in grape-growing regions with cool winters.

questions.explanation:
"Useless" is the conclusion. If the techniques can insert genes from cold-tolerant wild grapes, the research has value regardless of consumers' views on vegetable genes.
B — Untested suitability doesn't counter the claim; it may even support it.
C — Shows a need for cold tolerance but doesn't answer the consumer objection.
D — Labeling rules don't make the research useful.
E — Cool winters are not the very cold winters at issue.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q15
questions.stimulus:
Stephanie: The historic district should be expanded by several blocks immediately. The beauty of the nineteenth-century architecture on these blocks would draw more tourists to the city, and increased tourism would benefit all the residents due to the extra money coming into the community.
Shirley: Caution needs to be exercised. Rents would go up in apartment buildings on the fringes of the present historic district if it is expanded. This increase would seriously disrupt the lives of the people affected.
questions.stem: On the basis of their statements, Stephanie and Shirley are committed to disagreeing about the truth of which one of the following?

choices.A: The increased tourism in the expanded historic district would be a benefit to the city.
choices.B: Some of the residents of the expanded historic district would see their rents increase.
choices.C: Some people would be adversely affected by the expansion of the historic district.
choices.D: The historic district should not be expanded.
choices.E: The expansion of the historic district should be done without hesitation.

questions.explanation:
Stephanie says expand "immediately." Shirley says "caution needs to be exercised." They're committed to disagreeing about whether to proceed without hesitation.
A — Shirley doesn't dispute the tourism benefit.
B — Shirley's rent point is about the fringes of the present district, and Stephanie doesn't address rents.
C — Stephanie doesn't deny anyone could be hurt.
D — Shirley urges caution, not abandoning the expansion.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q16
questions.stimulus: Lawyer: In concluding that there were no witnesses to the crime, the investigators relied almost entirely on unverifiable claims. Thus, there is good reason to doubt the truth of their conclusion. But treating that reason for doubt as though it were proof that there were witnesses to the crime is equally unacceptable.
questions.stem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle illustrated above?

choices.A: A newspaper published an in-depth report of both sides of a dispute, without questioning the validity of either view. So, although the newspaper allowed each side to make its case, the report did not favor one side over the other.
choices.B: Although Ventola’s proposal appears to be a viable solution to the problem, we should not yet adopt her solution. There are undoubtedly many other solutions available, and we cannot know which solution is best until we have considered all of them.
choices.C: If a salesperson would receive a commission from selling a product, then it is reasonable to assume that the salesperson’s attitude toward the product might be biased. However, the mere possibility of bias should not be confused with actual bias.
choices.D: Ross has stated that he will never tell a lie, but that cannot be proven while Ross is still alive. After all, the truth of such a statement must be measured against actual events. Nonetheless, it would also be a mistake to take this to indicate that Ross will tell a lie.
choices.E: The makers of Ever Clean claim that Ever Clean is a better household cleaner than Total Clean because Total Clean is ineffective. It may be true that Total Clean is ineffective, but claims about Ever Clean’s efficacy should be based on Ever Clean’s performance.

questions.explanation:
Principle: a reason to doubt a claim isn't proof of its opposite. Ross's claim can't be proven, but that doesn't show he will lie.
A — About balanced reporting.
B — About considering alternatives before deciding.
C — Distinguishes possible bias from actual bias, close but not about treating doubt over a claim as proof of its negation.
E — About basing claims on the right evidence.

traps.E: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q17
questions.stimulus: Gala award ceremonies for theater and film artists can never succeed at their most obvious purpose—rewarding the best artists of a particular year. After all, judgments about an artist’s work are based largely on subjective preferences, and some brilliant artists who work outside the mainstream are not even considered for awards. Yet award ceremonies bring art to public awareness, a requirement for the advancement of culture in any society.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the statements above?

choices.A: The advancement of culture in any society requires that there be award ceremonies for theater and film artists.
choices.B: Some subjective judgments interfere with the advancement of culture in a society.
choices.C: An award ceremony for artists who work outside the mainstream would not advance culture in a society.
choices.D: Gala award ceremonies for theater and film artists are justified only if they reward the best artists of the particular year.
choices.E: The most obvious purpose behind gala award ceremonies for theater and film artists is not the best reason for holding them.

questions.explanation:
Ceremonies can never succeed at their obvious purpose (rewarding the best), yet they serve a needed cultural function. So the obvious purpose isn't the best reason to hold them.
A — Public awareness is required for culture, not award ceremonies specifically.
B — Not supported.
C — Not supported.
D — Would imply they're never justified, which conflicts with their stated value.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q18
questions.stimulus: Can everything be reduced to what is studied by physics? Many scientists think that such a reduction is only a matter of time. They argue that all phenomena can be adequately explained by the laws of physics alone. However, the science that is often mentioned as affording the best evidence for physical reductionism— psychology—also furnishes the critics of physical reductionism with their best examples of heretofore unreduced phenomena.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately and completely characterizes the role of the reference to psychology in the passage?

choices.A: It is presented as evidence that only in the distant future are reductions to what is studied by physics possible.
choices.B: It is given as an example of an area of science where reductions to what is studied by physics are common.
choices.C: It is used to show that attempts to effect a reduction to what is studied by physics, even in the best cases, are questionable.
choices.D: It is presented as an example of a scientific discipline that refutes the claims of the physical reductionists.
choices.E: It is used to illustrate the claim that the human sciences contain examples of unreduced phenomena.

questions.explanation:
Psychology is the reductionists' best evidence and also critics' best counterexamples. Even the best case is questionable.
A — No timeline claim.
B — It's cited as best evidence, but the point is that it also has unreduced phenomena.
D — "Refutes" is too strong.
E — Narrower than the point, and "human sciences" broadly isn't the claim.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q19
questions.stimulus: A minority political faction will gracefully accept the electoral victory of a majority if the two factions share many fundamental values. In such a case, the loss does not constitute a complete surrender of the losing faction’s vital interests. Hence, the cases in which majority rule works best include those in which each minority faction shares many fundamental values with the majority.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Majority rule is most successful when the political issues that are most widely discussed are not issues of fundamental values.
choices.B: If a minority political faction gracefully accepts the electoral victory of a majority, then the two factions share many fundamental values.
choices.C: Only if an electoral loss constitutes a complete surrender of a minority faction’s vital interests does majority rule work poorly.
choices.D: The cases in which majority rule works best include those in which every minority faction gracefully accepts the majority’s victory.
choices.E: Whenever minority and majority factions do not share many fundamental values, a minority faction’s electoral loss will constitute a complete surrender of its vital interests.

questions.explanation:
Shared values → graceful acceptance. Needed: majority rule works best in cases where every minority gracefully accepts. Then cases where every minority shares values are among those.
A — Which issues are discussed isn't linked.
B — Gives acceptance → shared values, the wrong direction.
C — Doesn't connect graceful acceptance to working best.
E — About not sharing values. Doesn't bridge to "works best."

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q20
questions.stimulus: Advertisement: If you own a car, you need collision insurance. And anyone who needs collision insurance wants the best insurance bargain available. So if you own a car, you will want to take advantage of Acme’s great rates on collision insurance.
questions.stem: The questionable pattern of reasoning in which one of the following arguments is most similar to that in the advertisement?

choices.A: Columnist: If you are unhappy with your career, you should pursue a new one. Anyone whose career does not provide interesting challenges should pursue a new one. Hence, if you are unhappy with your career, you should go into computer programming.
choices.B: Columnist: If you are pursuing a new career, you should consider one that provides interesting challenges. Anyone who goes into computer programming will have interesting challenges. So if you are pursuing a new career, you should consider computer programming.
choices.C: Columnist: You do not need to pursue a new career if you are happy with your current one. Everyone who pursues a new career should consider the challenging career of computer programming. Therefore, if you are happy with your current career, you should not consider computer programming.
choices.D: Columnist: Everyone who pursues a new career should seek one that provides the most interesting challenges. If you are unhappy with your career, you should pursue a new one. Thus, if you pursue a new career, you should go into computer programming.
choices.E: Columnist: You should pursue a new career if you are unhappy with your current one. Everyone who pursues a new career should seek the one that provides the most interesting challenges. So if you are unhappy with your current career, you should go into the challenging career of computer programming.

questions.explanation:
Ad: car → need insurance → want best bargain, so car → want Acme, silently assuming Acme is the best bargain. Columnist: unhappy → new career → most challenging, so unhappy → programming, assuming programming is most challenging.
A — Two separate reasons for a new career, then a leap. A different structure.
B — "Consider" a career with challenges, and programming has them. Much closer to valid.
C — Negates conditions. A different flaw.
D — Starts the chain at "pursue a new career," dropping the first link the original has.

traps.A: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure
traps.C: Describes the Topic, Not the Structure

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q21
questions.stimulus: Editorial: Politicians who accept large contributions from corporations are very likely to show favoritism toward those corporations. Mayor Thompson has consistently shown clear favoritism toward the Wycombe Corporation. So the mayor very likely accepted one or more contributions from that corporation.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the reasoning of the editorial’s argument?

choices.A: It proceeds as if the fact that people in a certain category are likely to be in another category establishes that a person in the latter category is likely to be in the former category.
choices.B: It fails to address the possibility that a specific member of a group is unrepresentative of that group in relevant respects.
choices.C: It treats a condition that is sufficient to establish the truth of the argument’s conclusion as a condition that must hold in order for the conclusion to be true.
choices.D: It fails to distinguish between the claim that two phenomena are consistently associated with each other and the claim that one of those phenomena is always causally responsible for the other.
choices.E: It rejects a claim by attacking a proponent of the claim rather than by addressing the claim itself.

questions.explanation:
Large contributions → likely favoritism doesn't mean favoritism → likely contributions. Favoritism has many causes.
B — Representativeness isn't the issue.
C — No sufficient/necessary mix-up is stated that way.
D — The argument doesn't assert causation as "always."
E — No attack on a proponent.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q22
questions.stimulus: Economist: Antagonism toward free trade and resulting attempts to restrict trade are on the rise in many countries of the world, primarily due to substantial increases in the inequality of incomes in those countries. Since free trade brings tremendous benefits to the economies of all participating countries, these countries should introduce reforms like more progressive income tax rates to achieve a significant redistribution of income.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the economist’s argument?

choices.A: Substantial increases in inequality of incomes in countries are not directly due to free trade.
choices.B: In countries with substantially unequal incomes, people with lower incomes receive little or no benefit from free trade.
choices.C: Restrictions on trade are one effective way to bring about significant redistribution of income in a country.
choices.D: The proposed policies to redistribute income in certain countries will not significantly undermine the economic benefits of free trade to those countries.
choices.E: Substantial redistribution of income in a country will increase the economic benefits that country receives from free trade.

questions.explanation:
The recommendation is to redistribute to protect free trade's benefits. If redistribution itself wrecked those benefits, the recommendation would defeat its purpose.
A — Even if trade caused the inequality, redistribution could still defuse antagonism.
B — Not required.
C — The economist wants to avoid restrictions.
E — Redistribution needs only preserve benefits, not increase them.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q23
questions.stimulus: Overall ketchup sales rose significantly when ketchup began to be sold in squeezable plastic containers, which made ketchup much easier to use. A paint manufacturer is considering packaging paint in plastic jugs. As was the case with ketchup in plastic containers, this is a smart marketing move.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument above?

choices.A: Before the introduction of squeezable ketchup containers, surveys showed that customers were dissatisfied with the difficulty of getting ketchup from the bottle.
choices.B: Many users find traditional paint cans difficult to store.
choices.C: Previous attempts to change paint packaging have often been well accepted by consumers.
choices.D: Changing the packaging of paint will create no greater manufacturing difficulties than were created by changing the packaging of ketchup.
choices.E: Packaging paint in plastic jugs will make paint easier to use.

questions.explanation:
The ketchup analogy works because plastic made it easier to use. If plastic jugs make paint easier to use, the analogy holds.
A — Supports the ketchup half, which is already given, not the paint half.
B — A storage benefit is a different reason from ease of use.
C — Past packaging changes don't show this one helps.
D — Manufacturing difficulty isn't the marketing logic.

questions.location: April 2025 LSAT Disclosure, Section 2 (Logical Reasoning), Q24
questions.stimulus: Researchers have found that when rivers are dammed, the number of plant species along their banks falls by an average of 15 percent. Thus it follows that if the Chiawatchee River is dammed, some plant species will disappear from its banks as a result.
questions.stem: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on which one of the following grounds?

choices.A: It overlooks the possibility that even if damming rivers inevitably contributes to reductions of an average of 15 percent in plant species, other factors may counteract the reductions in this number in specific instances.
choices.B: It fails to address adequately the possibility that the total number of plant species along the banks of a river need not fall even if some individual plant species disappear from the banks of that river.
